# Applicability conditions: how to tell whether a methodology fits

> Applicability conditions are the criteria in a carbon methodology that decide which project activities may use it, such as geography, technology, scale, dates and land-use history. A project must meet every condition, including those in referenced tools and modules, and justify each one separately in the project document. Validators test each condition against evidence.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/guides/applicability-conditions/

- **Defined in:** VCS Methodology Requirements, v5.0, section 3.2
- **Where they sit:** Section 4 of VCS methodologies, plus the conditions of every referenced tool and module
- **Assessed:** At validation, condition by condition, by the validation and verification body
- **VCS methodology deviations:** Monitoring and measurement only, never applicability
- **VM0047 v1.1 census-based density limit:** 50 planting units per hectare
- **VMR0017 v1.0 hydro limit:** 15 MW or less, least developed countries only

## What are applicability conditions, and where do they sit in a methodology?

Applicability conditions are the criteria in a methodology that decide which project activities may use it. Section 3.2 of the [VCS Methodology Requirements, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-methodology-requirements-v5-0/), gives geography, technology type and historical land use as examples. The same section says the conditions must not contain procedures or obligations. They are tests of eligibility, written so that eligibility can be determined at validation.

In VCS methodologies such as VM0047 and VMR0017 they sit in Section 4. [VM0047](https://climat.today/methodologies/vm0047/) version 1.1 splits them into general conditions, conditions for each quantification approach, and exclusion conditions. The list does not end there. Conditions set out in any tool or module the methodology uses also apply.

Geography can sit in a second place. Section 2.1.1 of the [VCS Standard, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v5-0/), sets default eligibility by location for certain activities, such as grid-connected wind and solar. A geographic condition in the methodology takes precedence over that default.

## Why must each condition be addressed explicitly in the project document?

The registry's template requires it, and the validator has to check the conditions one at a time. Verra's project description template tells the proponent to address each applicability condition separately, in a table that pairs the condition with a justification, repeated for every methodology, module and tool applied. Gold Standard's [Project Design Document template, v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/t-prereview-design-document/), has the same table, plus one for host country requirements.

A missing condition is not a small gap. Verra's [Validation and Verification Manual, v3.2](https://verra.org/documents/validation-and-verification-manual-v3-2/), treats failure to conform to any applicability condition as a material discrepancy.

Verra issued two templates on 9 June 2026, both effective 1 January 2027 according to its [rules page](https://verra.org/programs/verified-carbon-standard/vcs-program-details/). [Version 5.0A](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0a/) is for projects with a start date before 1 January 2027. [Version 5.0B](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0b/) is for projects starting on or after that date, and for earlier projects that renew or reassess the baseline from 1 January 2030. The applicability table is the same in both. For a submission before 2027, confirm on the rules page which template is in force that day.

## How do validators assess applicability conditions?

Condition by condition, against evidence. The Verra manual requires the validation and verification body (VVB) to assess the project against each condition. It dates from 2016, and the VCS Standard, v5.0, still directs VVBs to follow it.

Gold Standard spells out the method in paragraphs 7.12.4 to 7.12.6 of its [Validation and Verification Standard, v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/113-par-validation-and-verification-standard/). The VVB validates the documents cited in the design document, checks that they are correctly quoted and interpreted, cross-checks against other credible sources it knows of, describes the steps taken for each condition, and states an opinion. Gold Standard also screens earlier: under the [Principles & Requirements, v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/), the preliminary review covers the applicability of the methodology.

The VVB is not the last reader. Under the [Registration and Issuance Process, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/), Verra reviews every project request and can return or reject it.

## Which conditions are objective, and which need judgment?

A condition is objective when a number, a date or a published category settles it. It needs judgment when it turns on a description that the facts have to be matched to.

| Kind of condition | Example from a published methodology | What settles it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Threshold | Planting density does not exceed 50 planting units per hectare (VM0047 v1.1, census-based approach). | The census of planting units and the mapped area of the instance. |
| Threshold | Hydroelectric capacity of 15 MW or less (VMR0017 v1.0). | Rated or authorized capacity, whichever is higher. |
| Date or time window | Where site preparation starts the project, carbon stock estimates at time zero are set no more than two years before the start date (VM0047 v1.1, area-based approach). | Dated plot records. |
| Land-use history | The land was not managed forest at any point in the 10 years before the start date (VM0047 v1.1, area-based exclusion). | Evidence of land cover and management across the whole period. |
| Geography | Wind, geothermal and terrestrial solar PV only in low-, lower middle- and upper middle-income countries (VMR0017 v1.0). | The World Bank income classification. |
| Judgment | No woody biomass serving a similar purpose to the planting units was removed in the last 10 years (VM0047 v1.1, census-based exclusion). | Pre-project photos or an attestation, and a finding on what purpose the earlier vegetation served. |
| Judgment | A battery system and the power plant are part of the same investment decision (VMR0017 v1.0). | Ownership, financing and board records, read together. |

Objective conditions still rest on definitions. Continuous cropping in VM0047 means no fallow longer than one season, shown over 10 or more years before the start date. Where the text leaves room, the reading that counts is the VVB's and then the registry's, and neither is bound by a developer's interpretation.

## What can you do when a project fails one condition?

Under the VCS Program a failed applicability condition cannot be deviated from or exempted. The [VCS Standard, v4.7](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v4-7/), in section 3.20, and the VCS Standard, v5.0, in section 3.19, allow methodology deviations for monitoring and measurement only. Verra's [Exemption Request Procedure, v1.0](https://verra.org/documents/exemption-request-procedure-v1-0/), covers deadlines and VVB matters and nothing else. The real options are these:

1. **Check the input and the definition.** Conditions turn on defined terms, and the definition decides the result.

2. **Change the design.** VM0047 lets one project hold instances under different approaches, if each instance meets one approach in full and a buffer of at least 10 meters separates them.

3. **Use a different methodology.** It must be listed on the Verra website, in a version that is active on the date the request is submitted.

4. **Ask for a methodology revision.** The Methodology Requirements treat a revision as appropriate where the activity is broadly similar to eligible ones. Under the [Methodology Development and Review Process, v5.1](https://verra.org/documents/methodology-development-and-review-process-all/), Verra leads the work and a stakeholder starts it with a methodology idea note. A scope-expanding major revision must show potential of at least 500,000 tCO2e a year within five years.

Gold Standard has one more route. Its [Deviation Request Requirements and Procedures, v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/110-par-deviation-approval-procedure/), accept requests to deviate from a standard requirement or a methodology before submission. The Secretariat decides where a precedent exists. Otherwise the Technical Advisory Committee decides, which the document expects to take four to eight weeks. Decisions are published and approval is not assured. Permanent changes to a certified project go through the [Design Change Request Requirements and Procedures, v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/111-par-design-change-requirements/).

After registration, a VCS project that moves to another methodology follows the [Procedure to Change Methodology through a Project Description Deviation, v4.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-methodology-change-project-deviation-procedure-v4-0-1/). It must meet every applicability condition of the new methodology.

## How do the conditions work on a real project?

The two illustrations below use invented projects and the published text of each methodology.

### VM0047 v1.1, census-based approach

A developer plans to plant trees on 8 hectares of smallholder cropland at 45 planting units per hectare. Under [VM0047, v1.1](https://verra.org/documents/vm0047-afforestation-reforestation-and-revegetation-v1-1/), the density limit allows up to 400 units on this instance, so 360 passes. Section 4.3 asks for less than 10% pre-existing woody biomass cover, and/or continuous cropping or a settlements or other lands category. Section 6.2 asks for the cover limit and one of those land uses together, so the developer should evidence both. Soil inversion for planting must stay within 25 cm and happen only once in the crediting period. Records and measurements settle these.

Two conditions need a person. Planting must be dispersed across the instance, not concentrated in part of it. And the pre-project land use must be maintained for the project lifetime, which is a claim about the future. At 80 units per hectare the instance fails the census-based approach and would have to meet the area-based conditions instead.

### VMR0017 v1.0

A 40 MW onshore wind farm is planned in a lower middle-income country that is not a least developed country. The default eligibility in the VCS Standard, v5.0, admits grid-connected wind only in least developed countries. [VMR0017, v1.0](https://verra.org/documents/vmr0017-grid-connected-electricity-generation-from-renewable-sources/), admits wind of any capacity in low-, lower middle- and upper middle-income countries, and states that its condition supersedes the default. The project passes. The same plant in a high-income country fails. A 20 MW hydroelectric plant fails everywhere, because hydro is limited to 15 MW and to least developed countries.

VMR0017 does not stand alone. It must be used with CDM methodology ACM0002, v22.0, and its tools carry their own conditions. Verra's [methodology page](https://verra.org/methodologies/vmr0017-grid-connected-electricity-generation-from-renewable-sources-acm0002-revision-v1-0/) states that projects requesting registration on or after 1 January 2027 must apply VMR0017 in full.

## How Climat handles this

Climat's applicability check evaluates every applicability condition of the chosen methodology as pass, fail or needs review. Conditions that call for judgment are routed to a person instead of being guessed. The methodologies available today are Verra VM0047 v1.1, census-based approach, and Verra VMR0017 v1.0.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a methodology deviation fix a failed applicability condition?

Not under the VCS Program. Both the VCS Standard, v4.7, and the VCS Standard, v5.0, permit methodology deviations only for monitoring and measurement and state that deviations from any other part of the methodology are not permitted. Gold Standard has a separate deviation request process, decided case by case.

### Do the applicability conditions of tools and modules count?

Yes. The VCS Methodology Requirements, v5.0, state that applicability conditions set out in tools or modules used by a methodology also apply. Verra's project description template asks for a separate table for each methodology, module and tool applied.

### When are applicability conditions assessed?

At validation. The VCS Methodology Requirements, v5.0, require conditions to be written so that eligibility can be determined at validation, without ongoing actions to stay eligible. A later change to the project that affects applicability is handled as a project description deviation and assessed at verification.

### Does a methodology's geographic condition override the VCS Standard's default eligibility?

Yes. Section 2.1.1 of the VCS Standard, v5.0, says a geographic applicability condition in a methodology takes precedence over the default eligibility in Table 1. VMR0017 v1.0 states that its technology and geography table supersedes that default.

### Can Verra grant an exemption from an applicability condition?

No. Verra's Exemption Request Procedure, v1.0, allows exemption requests only for deadlines, site visits by the validation and verification body, rotation and change of that body. It states that requests related to any other program rules will not be granted.

### What happens if a registered project stops meeting a condition?

Under the VCS Standard the change is a project description deviation. Where it affects the applicability of the methodology, the proponent describes and justifies it in a revised project description, and the validation and verification body assesses it at the next verification. Both the VCS Standard, v4.7, and the VCS Standard, v5.0, require a site visit at that verification.

# How to register a carbon project

> Registering a carbon project follows one sequence under Verra VCS and Gold Standard: select a methodology, list the project, consult stakeholders, pass validation by an approved validation/verification body, and pass the registry's review. Credits are issued later, after monitoring and verification. Verra calls the approval registration; Gold Standard calls it design certification.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/guides/how-to-register-a-carbon-project/

- **Verra VCS public comment period:** 30 days, starting when the project is listed as under validation
- **Gold Standard first submission:** Preliminary review within one year of the project start date
- **Gold Standard validation deadline:** Within two years of listing
- **Verra fees (Fee Schedule v1.2):** USD 1,500 pipeline listing, USD 3,750 registration review, USD 0.23 per tCO2e issuance levy
- **Gold Standard fees (Fee Schedule v3.1):** USD 1,000 preliminary review, USD 2,500 design review, USD 2,000 performance review
- **VCS version in force:** Version 5 released 16 December 2025; VCS Standard v4.7 active until 1 January 2027

## What are the steps to register a carbon project?

The order is the same under Verra and Gold Standard: select a methodology, list the project, consult the public, have a validation/verification body (VVB) validate the design, and pass the registry's review. Credits come later, after monitoring, verification and an issuance request.

The names differ. Verra registers a project. Gold Standard certifies the design, and later certifies performance.

| Stage | Verra VCS | Gold Standard for the Global Goals |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Listing | Pipeline listing, as under development or under validation | Preliminary review, then Listed status |
| Public input | 30-day public comment period | Stakeholder consultation in two rounds, plus a two-week public consultation in each Gold Standard review |
| Design audit | Validation | Validation |
| Registry decision | Project review, then registration | Design review, then Certified Design status |
| Results audit | Verification | Verification |
| Credits | Verified Carbon Units (VCUs) | Verified Emission Reductions (VERs) |

## Which version of the rules applies?

Under Verra, two versions overlap until the end of 2026. Verra released VCS Version 5 on 16 December 2025, and its [rules page](https://verra.org/programs/verified-carbon-standard/vcs-program-details/) lists the VCS Standard v4.7 as active until 1 January 2027. The [overview of updates and effective dates](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-version-5-overview-of-vcs-program-updates-and-effective-dates/) gives a date for each change. Updates are effective immediately unless the overview says otherwise. Most design requirements apply to requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027. The new stakeholder engagement and safeguard requirements apply to projects with a start date on or after 1 January 2027.

The steps below name the version behind each rule. Gold Standard's [Principles & Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/) have been effective since 5 December 2024.

## How do you register a project under Verra VCS?

Section numbers refer to the [Registration and Issuance Process v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/) (RIP), the [VCS Standard v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v5-0/) and the [VCS Standard v4.7](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v4-7/). Fees come from the [Verra Program Fee Schedule v1.2](https://verra.org/documents/verra-program-fee-schedule-v1-2/) of 15 September 2026.

1. **Feasibility and methodology selection.** The developer selects a methodology listed on Verra's website and checks the project against every [applicability condition](https://climat.today/guides/applicability-conditions/). The version applied must be active on the date the registration request is submitted (VCS Standard v5.0, section 3.1.4). Verra's part is to publish the list of active methodologies.

2. **Registry account.** The developer applies for a Verra Registry account, which can be done at any time (RIP, section 2.1.3). Verra reviews the application. Opening costs USD 750 and annual maintenance USD 750.

3. **Pipeline listing.** The developer submits a listing representation with either a draft project description, to list as under development, or a complete one with proof of VVB contracting, to list as under validation (RIP, sections 3.1.5 to 3.1.7). The fee is USD 1,500. Verra may review the documents, and issues must be addressed within 90 days or the project is inactivated (section 3.1.13). For requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027, the [Corrections and Clarifications of 9 June 2026](https://verra.org/documents/corrections-and-clarifications-cc-to-the-vcs-program-rules-published-9-june-2026/) add a stakeholder engagement plan and an ESG risk assessment, with exceptions for projects that started earlier.

4. **Public comment.** Listing as under validation opens a 30-day public comment period (RIP, section 3.1.17). Verra shares the comments and posts a public summary. The developer must take due account of them before validation is finalized (VCS Standard v5.0, section 3.17.20), and the VVB evaluates the response.

5. **Validation.** A [Verra-approved VVB](https://verra.org/validation-verification/) assesses the [project description](https://climat.today/guides/what-is-a-pdd/), visits the site, raises findings, and issues a validation report and a validation representation.

6. **Registration request and Verra review.** The developer submits the project description, the validation report, the representations, evidence of ownership or of the right to operate, and supporting documents (RIP, section 4.2.3), and pays USD 3,750. Verra sends any findings to the VVB in a project review report. The VVB has 90 days to respond, Verra may run up to three review rounds, and the request is approved or returned (section 4.3).

7. **Monitoring.** The developer implements the monitoring plan and prepares a monitoring report for a distinct monitoring period (VCS Standard v5.0, section 3.4.5).

8. **Verification.** A VVB verifies the report to a reasonable level of assurance, with a site visit at the first verification (VCS Standard v5.0, sections 4.1.9 and 4.1.11). The developer then requests verification approval and pays USD 5,000, of which USD 2,500 is credited against issuance.

9. **Issuance.** After approval, the registry generates serial numbers and invoices the issuance levy of USD 0.23 per tCO2e claimed. VCUs are deposited once the levy is paid (RIP, section 4.4.5). AFOLU and geological storage projects also deposit buffer credits according to their non-permanence risk rating (section 5.1).

### What are the Verra deadlines?

The deadlines changed with Version 5, and so did the date they count from. Version 4.7 counts from the project start date. Version 5.0 counts from the initial crediting period start date, the date on which reductions or removals begin to occur.

| Rule | VCS Standard v4.7, section 3.8 | VCS Standard v5.0, sections 3.8.2 and 3.8.3 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pipeline listing | AFOLU projects: within three years | All projects: within one year |
| Non-AFOLU projects (v4.7); energy and industry and geological carbon storage projects (v5.0) | Complete validation within two years | Submit the registration request within two years |
| The same projects, where they apply a new VCS methodology | Complete validation within four years, and within two years of the methodology's approval | Submit the registration request within four years, and within two years of the methodology's approval (energy and industry projects) |
| AFOLU projects | Complete validation within five years | Submit the registration request within five years |
| ARR, RWE and IFM projects (except logged to protected forest), and AFOLU projects of 20,000 tCO2e per year or less | Complete validation within eight years | Submit the registration request within eight years |

The v5.0 registration deadlines apply to requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027, except for projects already listed as under validation on or before 16 December 2025. The v5.0 listing deadline applies to listing requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027. From the same date, a project that does not request verification approval within five years of registration or of its last verification approval is marked late to verify (RIP, sections 4.1.2 and 4.7.1).

## How do you register a project under Gold Standard?

Section numbers refer to the Principles & Requirements v2.1 unless stated. Fees come from the [Gold Standard Fee Schedule v3.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/fees/) of 28 July 2025. Gold Standard also publishes the sequence in its [certification process step-by-step](https://www.goldstandard.org/publications/certification-process-stepbystep).

1. **Feasibility and methodology selection.** The developer confirms that the project type is eligible, selects an approved methodology, and checks the activity requirements and safeguarding principles. The developer opens an Impact Registry account, which costs USD 1,000 a year per organization.

2. **Stakeholder consultation.** The developer runs at least two rounds: a physical meeting, with invitations sent at least 30 days before, and a feedback round lasting at least 30 days ([Stakeholder Consultation and Engagement Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/102-par-stakeholder-consultation-requirements/), sections 3.4.2 and 3.6.1). Consultation is due before the project start date.

3. **Preliminary review and listing.** Within one year of the project start date, the developer submits the key project information, a draft stakeholder consultation report, a signed cover letter and the terms and conditions, and pays USD 1,000 (sections 4.1.49 and 5.1.7). Land use and forests projects follow their own timeline. Gold Standard runs a completeness check within 14 days of submission and payment, and lists the project on the Impact Registry if it passes (section 5.1.4). Listed status is not certification (section 5.1.12).

4. **Validation.** The developer contracts a VVB from the [approved list](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/verification-validation-bodies/), hands over the complete PDD and stakeholder consultation report, and notifies Gold Standard that validation has started (section 5.1.13). Validation must be completed within two years of listing (section 5.1.16).

5. **Design review.** The developer pays USD 2,500. Gold Standard reviews the documents and the validation report for a minimum of four weeks, including a two-week public consultation (sections 5.1.19 to 5.1.21). Responses to findings are due within six weeks (section 5.1.22). A positive result gives Certified Design status.

6. **Monitoring.** The developer follows the Monitoring & Reporting Plan and files an annual report for each monitoring year in which verification is not completed (section 5.1.39). Missing annual reports lead to de-certification (section 5.1.40).

7. **Verification.** The VVB verifies the monitoring report. A physical site visit is mandatory at the first verification ([GHG Emissions Reduction & Sequestration Product Requirements v3.2](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/501-pr-ghg-emissions-reductions-sequestration/), section 12.1.4). The first verification must be completed within two years of the implementation date or of design certification, whichever is later (section 5.1.29).

8. **Performance review and issuance.** The developer pays USD 2,000. Gold Standard reviews for a minimum of three weeks, including a two-week public consultation (section 5.1.34). Credits are then issued on payment of the issuance fee: USD 0.25 per credit, or USD 0.15 per credit plus 2 percent of the issuance. Rates are lower for projects in least developed countries.

9. **Renewal.** Certification runs in five-year cycles. To continue, the VVB's renewal opinion must reach Gold Standard no later than the last day of the current cycle (section 5.1.45).

## How long does registration take?

Neither registry publishes a total duration. Most of the elapsed time depends on the developer's evidence and the VVB's schedule, and VVB fees are contracted directly with the VVB. The published periods are these.

- **Verra.** A 30-day public comment period, and 90 days for responses to findings. Section 4.3 of the RIP states no duration for Verra's own review.

- **Gold Standard.** A completeness check within 14 days at preliminary review, a design review of at least four weeks, and a performance review of at least three weeks. Each review ends only when all corrective action requests and clarification requests are closed.

For what happens inside the audit, see [validation and verification](https://climat.today/guides/validation-and-verification/).

## How Climat handles this

A project in Climat starts by choosing a registry and a methodology, and the [applicability check](https://climat.today/product/applicability-check/) evaluates every applicability condition of that methodology as pass, fail or needs review. Climat then [drafts each section](https://climat.today/product/document-drafting/) of the registry's project document in the registry's own order. Climat is not a registry and not a validation body, it does not guarantee registration, and monitoring periods after registration are in development.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a project have to be listed before validation starts?

Yes, under both registries. Under section 4.1.5 of the VCS Standard v5.0, the project must be listed on the pipeline as under validation before the opening meeting, and validation cannot be completed until the 30-day public comment period has ended. Under Gold Standard's Principles & Requirements v2.1, validation may start only after the project has achieved Listed status.

### Can validation and the first verification be done together?

Yes. The VCS Standard v5.0 allows validation before or at the same time as the first verification, and the Registration and Issuance Process v5.0 allows registration and verification review to be requested together. Gold Standard allows design certification to be combined with the first performance certification, in which case its review lasts a minimum of six weeks.

### How much does it cost to register a carbon project with Verra?

The Verra Program Fee Schedule v1.2 of 15 September 2026 sets USD 750 to open a registry account and USD 750 a year to maintain it, USD 1,500 for pipeline listing, USD 3,750 for registration review, and USD 5,000 for each verification review, of which USD 2,500 is credited against issuance. The issuance levy is USD 0.23 per tonne of CO2e claimed. Validation/verification body fees are separate.

### What happens if Verra returns a registration request?

Verra notifies the proponent and posts any project review report on the registry. The proponent may address the reasons and submit a new request, and pays the review fee again. A new request submitted within 180 days may use the same versions of the program documents, methodology and templates. If none is submitted within one year, Verra inactivates the project.

### What is a retroactive project under Gold Standard?

A project whose first round of stakeholder consultation takes place after the project start date. It stays eligible only if it is submitted for preliminary review within one year of the start date. The developer must explain why consultation came late and how the comments were taken into account.

# Validation vs verification in carbon projects

> Validation is the independent assessment of a carbon project's design before registration. Verification is the periodic, after-the-fact assessment of the emission reductions or removals the project reports. A validation/verification body approved by the registry performs both, raises findings that the developer must close, and issues a report and opinion that the registry then reviews.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/guides/validation-and-verification/

- **Validation assesses:** The project design and its forecast, before registration
- **Verification assesses:** Monitored results for a past monitoring period
- **Finding types under Verra and Gold Standard:** Corrective action request (CAR), clarification request (CL), forward action request (FAR)
- **Verra VVB accreditation:** By an IAF member accreditation body with IAF MLA recognition under ISO 17029 and/or ISO 14065, plus Verra approval
- **Gold Standard VVB accreditation:** ISO 14065 under the ANSI-GS Accreditation Program, or UNFCCC CDM or Article 6.4 accreditation, plus Gold Standard approval
- **VCS materiality threshold:** 1 percent for large projects (over 300,000 tCO2e per year), 5 percent otherwise

## What is the difference between validation and verification?

Validation assesses the design of a project before it is registered. Verification assesses the results after they have occurred. An independent validation/verification body (VVB) carries out both.

Verra's [VCS Program Definitions v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-program-definitions-v5-0/) define validation as the independent assessment of whether the project conforms to the VCS Program rules, including the reasonableness of the assumptions, limitations and methods behind a claim about future outcomes. They define verification as the periodic ex-post assessment of the reductions and removals that occurred during the monitoring period, based on historical data.

| Question | Validation | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is assessed | The project design, in the [project description or PDD](https://climat.today/guides/what-is-a-pdd/) | The results, in the monitoring report |
| Nature of the evidence | Forecasts and assumptions | Historical data |
| When | Before registration, and again at crediting period or certification renewal | For each monitoring period |
| Registry decision that follows | Registration (Verra) or design certification (Gold Standard) | Verification approval and issuance (Verra) or performance certification and issuance (Gold Standard) |
| Site visit | Verra: required. Gold Standard: a physical visit is not mandatory. | Both: required at the first verification. |

The site visit rules come from sections 4.1.10 and 4.1.11 of the [VCS Standard v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v5-0/), unchanged in substance from v4.7, and from section 12.1.4 of Gold Standard's [GHG Emissions Reduction & Sequestration Product Requirements v3.2](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/501-pr-ghg-emissions-reductions-sequestration/).

## What is a validation/verification body?

A VVB is an independent third-party auditor approved by the registry. The developer appoints and contracts it. The registry approves it, oversees its work and can sanction it.

The [VCS Program Guide v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-program-guide-v5-0/) (sections 2.6.5 and 6) gives Verra the power to review a VVB's work, witness its audits, report its performance to the accreditation body, and suspend it. Gold Standard's [Validation and Verification Body Requirements v3.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/109-par-validation-verification-body-requirements/) make the VVB responsible for the certification decision and Gold Standard responsible for managing the process.

A VVB does not advise on the projects it audits. Verra's [Validation and Verification Manual v3.2](https://verra.org/documents/validation-and-verification-manual-v3-2/) tells VVBs not to offer consulting advice when they issue findings. Gold Standard bars VVBs from consultancy on Gold Standard projects (section 8.7.1.5).

## How are VVBs approved under Verra and Gold Standard?

Both registries require an external accreditation first and their own approval second. Approval is granted by sectoral scope, so a VVB approved for energy projects cannot audit a forestry project on that basis.

| Requirement | Verra VCS | Gold Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accreditation | By an accreditation body that is a member of the International Accreditation Forum (IAF) and recognized under the IAF Multilateral Recognition Arrangement for ISO 17029 and/or ISO 14065 (Program Guide v5.0, section 5) | ISO 14065 accreditation for greenhouse gas activities under the ANSI-GS Accreditation Program, or UNFCCC accreditation under the CDM or the Article 6.4 mechanism (VVB Requirements v3.0, section 7.4.1) |
| Registry approval | Approval by Verra, active listing on Verra's website, and a signed agreement | Desk-based assessment by the Gold Standard Secretariat, granted for 36 months (section 9.2.2) |
| Auditors | The team must meet the competence requirements of ISO 14065 (VCS Standard v5.0, section 4.1.17) | Named auditors must pass Gold Standard's exam with a score above 75 percent (section 9.4.2.3) |
| Annual fee paid by the VVB | USD 5,000 for one Verra program ([Fee Schedule v1.2](https://verra.org/documents/verra-program-fee-schedule-v1-2/)) | USD 2,500 ([Fee Schedule v3.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/fees/)) |

Verra's [VVB page](https://verra.org/validation-verification/) lists the approved bodies and the recognized accreditation bodies. It notes that some previously approved UNFCCC-accredited bodies may hold an extension to use that accreditation until they receive ISO 14065 accreditation. Verra's [rules page](https://verra.org/programs/verified-carbon-standard/vcs-program-details/) lists the VCS Program Guide v4.4 as active until 1 January 2027 alongside v5.0.

On the audit itself, section 4.1.1 of the VCS Standard v5.0 requires validation and verification to be carried out in conformance to ISO 14064-3 and ISO 14065. Gold Standard sets its own rules in its [Validation and Verification Standard v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/113-par-validation-and-verification-standard/), in force since 5 December 2024.

## What happens in a validation?

A validation moves from planning to a desk review, a site visit, findings, closure and a report. The registry's own review follows.

1. **Contract and notice.** The developer contracts an approved VVB. Under Verra the project must be listed as under validation before the opening meeting (VCS Standard v5.0, section 4.1.5). Under Gold Standard the project must be Listed, and the developer notifies Gold Standard that validation has started ([Principles & Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/), section 5.1.13).

2. **Planning.** The VVB assesses the risk of material error and prepares a sampling plan and a validation plan. Verra's manual treats these plans as living documents that change as evidence comes in.

3. **Desk review.** The VVB reviews the project document and the supporting evidence and cross-checks them against other sources. Gold Standard states that the evidence is not limited to what the developer provides (Validation and Verification Standard v2.0, paragraph 6.2.1).

4. **Site visit and interviews.** The VVB visits facilities or project areas and interviews staff and stakeholders. Under Verra the audit team selects the stakeholders independently (VCS Standard v5.0, section 4.1.14). Where a Gold Standard VVB does not inspect on site, it must describe the alternative means and justify them (paragraph 6.3.4).

5. **Findings.** The VVB issues its findings in writing.

6. **Closure.** The developer answers each finding by changing the design, correcting the document, or supplying explanations or evidence. The VVB decides whether the answer closes it.

7. **Technical review and report.** Gold Standard requires a technical review of the final draft by a team separate from the auditors before the report is issued (VVB Requirements v3.0, section 8.4). The VVB then issues the validation report and opinion.

8. **Registry review.** Verra may send findings to the VVB in a project review report. The VVB has 90 days to respond and Verra may run up to three rounds ([Registration and Issuance Process v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/), section 4.3). Gold Standard's design review lasts at least four weeks, and responses to its findings are due within six weeks.

Under Verra, validation cannot be completed until the 30-day public comment period has ended. The sequence around the audit is in [how to register a carbon project](https://climat.today/guides/how-to-register-a-carbon-project/).

## What types of findings are there?

Verra and Gold Standard use the same three: the corrective action request, the clarification request and the forward action request. The definitions below are Gold Standard's, from paragraphs 6.3.14 to 6.3.17 of its Validation and Verification Standard v2.0.

| Finding | When it is raised | What closes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corrective action request (CAR) | A mistake affects the project's ability to achieve real, measurable, verifiable and additional reductions; a requirement has not been met; or there is a risk that reductions cannot be monitored or calculated | A change to the project design, a corrected document, or explanations or evidence that satisfy the VVB |
| Clarification request (CL) | Information is insufficient or not clear enough to determine whether a requirement has been met | The same |
| Forward action request (FAR) | An issue of project implementation needs review at the first verification. It cannot concern a requirement for design certification | Review at a later verification. If unresolved, the VVB considers converting it to a CAR |

Verra's manual defines a CL as a case where reporting lacks transparency and more information is needed, and a CAR as a material discrepancy or non-conformance. It requires every CL and CAR to be resolved before a positive opinion. The [VCS Validation Report Template v5.0A](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-validation-report-template-v5-0a/) requires the VVB to list every CAR, CL and FAR. The VCS documents read for this guide use the term FAR without defining it.

Gold Standard's own reviews can also raise non-conformities and observations (Principles & Requirements v2.1, section 5.1.10).

## How can developers prepare so fewer findings are raised?

Prepare for the checks the standards tell the VVB to make. No registry publishes data on how far any one measure reduces findings, so treat this list as a reading of the rules, not a guarantee.

- **Check the deadline and the methodology version before contracting.** Verra's manual asks VVBs to confirm both in a pre-validation assessment.

- **Hand over a complete file.** Gold Standard lets validation start only after the VVB has the full project documentation and supporting documents.

- **Cite a source for every value.** The VVB cross-checks the document against outside sources.

- **Keep the documents consistent.** Gold Standard requires figures to align across the PDD, the stakeholder consultation report, the SDG Impact Tool and the validation report (paragraph 7.16.6).

- **Answer public comments in writing.** The VVB evaluates the response (VCS Standard v5.0, section 4.1.6).

- **Do not expect the VVB to propose the fix.** It is not allowed to consult.

## What do the final validation report and statement contain?

The report records the process, the findings and their resolution, and the VVB's opinion. Both registries prescribe a template.

The VCS template has four parts: introduction, validation process, validation findings and validation opinion. Appendices list every finding and the competence of the team. Under section 4.1.24 of the VCS Standard v5.0, the opinion must state its date, the project name, the GHG statement and the period it covers, and that the statement is the responsibility of the project proponent. It must identify the objectives, scope and criteria, say whether the data are hypothetical, projected or historical, and give the VVB's conclusion. For a forecast, it must explain that actual results may differ. The VVB also signs a validation representation, a deed that accompanies the report.

Gold Standard's [validation report template v1.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/t-paa-vvb-project-activity-validation-report/) dates from 15 May 2026. Under paragraphs 7.16.3 to 7.16.6 of the Validation and Verification Standard v2.0, the report carries a positive or negative decision, a statement on the likelihood of achieving the estimated reductions and SDG impacts, the responses to CARs and CLs, the FARs identified, the documents reviewed, the interviewees, and the audit team.

## How Climat handles this

Climat's evidence gap report lists what the project still has to prove, most serious first, before any drafting starts. A [pre-validation review](https://climat.today/product/pre-validation/) that reads the finished draft adversarially is in development. Climat is not a validation body, and it does not replace validation or verification.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can the same VVB validate and verify a project?

Under section 4.1.27 of the VCS Standard v5.0, the same VVB may do the initial validation and the first verification, the next verification must go to a different VVB, and no VVB may verify more than six consecutive years of a project's reductions or removals. Gold Standard allows the same VVB to do both unless a methodology or product requirement says otherwise. Its Validation and Verification Standard v2.0 then requires a different audit team for the verification, except where design certification and the first verification are combined.

### Is a site visit required for validation?

Under Verra, yes: section 4.1.10 of the VCS Standard v5.0 requires a site visit at validation and at crediting period renewal. Under Gold Standard, a physical site visit is not mandatory at validation but is mandatory at the first verification, and the first physical visit must take place within two years of the project start date.

### What is the difference between a CAR and a CL?

A corrective action request says something is wrong: a requirement has not been met or an error affects the claimed reductions. A clarification request says the information is insufficient or unclear, so the auditor cannot yet tell whether the requirement is met. Both must be closed before a positive validation opinion is issued.

### Can a project be approved with an open forward action request?

Yes. Under Gold Standard's Validation and Verification Standard v2.0, a FAR flags an implementation issue for review at the first verification and is reported in the validation report. It cannot be used for a requirement the project must meet to achieve design certification. If it is still unresolved at verification, it becomes grounds for a corrective action request.

### Does the registry repeat the validation?

No. Verra reviews whether the VVB has appropriately assessed the project and fully described that assessment, and its Program Guide v5.0 states that reviews do not replace validation or verification. Gold Standard reviews every positive report with at least one expert reviewer and may raise further findings, but it cannot overturn a negative opinion from a VVB.

4. [Registration and Issuance Process, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)
5. [Validation and Verification Manual, v3.2](https://verra.org/documents/validation-and-verification-manual-v3-2/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)
6. [VCS Validation Report Template, v5.0A](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-validation-report-template-v5-0a/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)
7. [Validation and Verification (VVB eligibility and approved bodies)](https://verra.org/validation-verification/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)
8. [Verra Program Fee Schedule, v1.2](https://verra.org/documents/verra-program-fee-schedule-v1-2/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)
9. [VCS Program rules and requirements (list of current documents and templates)](https://verra.org/programs/verified-carbon-standard/vcs-program-details/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)
10. [Validation and Verification Standard, v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/113-par-validation-and-verification-standard/), Gold Standard (accessed 2026-09-29)

URL: https://climat.today/guides/verra-vs-gold-standard/

# Verra vs Gold Standard for project developers

> Verra's Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) covers all seven Kyoto Protocol gases and project types such as avoided deforestation and geological carbon storage. Gold Standard for the Global Goals credits only carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, requires two rounds of stakeholder consultation, and certifies projects in five-year cycles. Deadlines, buffers, labels and fees also differ.

Updated 2026-09-30. Canonical: https://climat.today/guides/verra-vs-gold-standard/

- **Rules compared:** VCS Standard v5.0 and v4.7, Gold Standard Principles & Requirements v2.1
- **Eligible gases:** VCS: seven Kyoto Protocol gases and ozone-depleting substances. Gold Standard: CO2, CH4 and N2O only
- **Public input:** VCS: 30-day public comment period. Gold Standard: two consultation rounds, then a two-week public consultation
- **Validation deadline:** VCS v4.7: two, five or eight years from the project start date. Gold Standard: two years from listing
- **Buffer for land use projects:** VCS: risk rating of 12 to 60 from the AFOLU tool. Gold Standard: 20% of issued credits
- **Issuance fee:** Verra: USD 0.23 per tCO2e claimed. Gold Standard: USD 0.25 per credit, or USD 0.15 plus 2% of the issuance

## How do Verra VCS and Gold Standard compare?

Verra's Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) has the wider scope. Gold Standard for the Global Goals credits three gases and five project types, and sets fixed minimums for stakeholder consultation. Both list a project, have a validation/verification body (VVB) audit it, and review the audit before registration.

Verra released VCS Version 5 on 16 December 2025. Its [overview of effective dates](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-version-5-overview-of-vcs-program-updates-and-effective-dates/) applies most design rules to requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027, so the table names the version behind each VCS rule.

| Topic | Verra VCS | Gold Standard for the Global Goals |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | Reductions of the seven Kyoto Protocol gases and ozone-depleting substances, and removals of CO2 ([VCS Program Guide, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-program-guide-v5-0/)) | CO2, CH4 and N2O only, in five listed project types ([GHG Emissions Reduction & Sequestration Product Requirements, v3.2](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/501-pr-ghg-emissions-reductions-sequestration/)) |
| Project document | Project description in five sections, on [template v5.0A](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0a/) or [v5.0B](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0b/) | Project Design Document in sections A to I, on [template v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/t-prereview-design-document/) |
| Sustainable development | Contributions to at least three SDGs ([VCS Standard, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v5-0/), section 3.16) | Positive impacts on at least three SDGs, one of them SDG 13 ([Principles & Requirements, v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/)) |
| Safeguards | Risk assessment and mitigation under section 3.19 of the [VCS Standard, v4.7](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v4-7/). v5.0 requires an ESG risk assessment before the project start date | Assessment against nine principles ([Safeguarding Principles & Requirements, v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/103-par-safeguarding-principles-requirements/)) |
| Consultation | Stakeholder consultation, then a 30-day public comment period ([Registration and Issuance Process, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/)) | A physical meeting and a feedback round of at least 30 days ([Stakeholder Consultation and Engagement Requirements, v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/102-par-stakeholder-consultation-requirements/)), then a two-week public consultation |
| Crediting period | v5.0: five years, renewable twice, for energy and industry, and 20 to 100 years for most land use projects. v4.7: seven years, renewable twice, or ten years fixed | Five-year certification cycles: 15 years for renewable energy and community services, 30 to 50 years for afforestation and reforestation |
| Deadline | v4.7: complete validation within two, five or eight years of the project start date. v5.0: request registration within the same periods, counted from the initial crediting period start date | Preliminary review within one year of the project start date, validation within two years of listing |
| Reversal risk | Pooled buffer sized by a risk rating of 12 to 60 ([Procedure for Applying the AFOLU Non-Permanence Risk Tool, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/procedure-for-applying-the-afolu-non-permanence-risk-tool-v5-0/)) | 20% of the credits issued to land use and forests projects |
| Buyer labels | CCP, CORSIA and Article 6 labels on Verified Carbon Units (VCUs) | CCP, CORSIA and Article 6 labels on Gold Standard Verified Emission Reductions (GSVERs) |
| Registry fees | Listing USD 1,500, registration review USD 3,750, issuance USD 0.23 per tCO2e ([Verra Program Fee Schedule, v1.2](https://verra.org/documents/verra-program-fee-schedule-v1-2/)) | Preliminary review USD 1,000, design review USD 2,500, issuance USD 0.25 per credit ([Gold Standard Fee Schedule, v3.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/fees/)) |

A proponent may choose to be validated to Version 5 before its effective dates. The project must then conform to all Version 5 requirements, except those whose effective date depends on the project start date or the listing date.

## Which project types can each registry take?

Project type settles the choice for many developers, because Gold Standard excludes more. Check the gas, the activity and the host country first.

- **VCS scope.** Table 8 of the VCS Standard, v5.0, names project types from energy and industry to reduced deforestation (REDD), improved forest management, wetland restoration and geological carbon storage.

- **VCS limits.** Table 1 of the same standard makes six activities eligible by default only in least developed countries. They include grid-connected wind, geothermal and solar photovoltaic plants, and hydropower of 15 MW or less. A methodology's own geographic conditions take precedence: [VMR0017, v1.0](https://verra.org/documents/vmr0017-grid-connected-electricity-generation-from-renewable-sources/), opens wind, geothermal and terrestrial solar projects to low, lower-middle and upper-middle income countries.

- **Gold Standard scope.** The product requirements list renewable energy supply, end-use energy efficiency, waste handling and disposal, land use and forests, and carbon dioxide removal. The [Land Use & Forests Activity Requirements, v1.2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/203-ar-luf-activity-requirements/), name two eligible types: afforestation and reforestation, and agriculture.

- **Gold Standard limits.** The Principles & Requirements exclude geo-engineering, energy from fossil fuel or nuclear, and fossil fuel switch. Under the [Renewable Energy Activity Requirements, v1.4](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/202-ar-renewable-energy-activity-requirements/), a grid-connected project must be in a least developed country, a small island developing state or a landlocked developing country, or in a low or lower-middle income country where the technology is under 5% of grid capacity. Exceptions are listed.

A type that Gold Standard does not list can be submitted for approval at preliminary review. New projects face one more test in 2026. Under the [Requirements for Paris Agreement Alignment, v1.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/119_paa_pr_100-01-requirements-paris-agreement-alignment/), a project submitted for preliminary review after 30 June 2026 must use a Paris Agreement-aligned methodology.

## What differs in the documents?

Both registries want the same underlying case — the activity is eligible, it is additional, the baseline is credible, the numbers are right, and the monitoring will hold up. They ask for it in different shapes, and the shape is what a developer actually has to work in.

Verra's project description is written on [template v5.0A](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0a/) or [v5.0B](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0b/): five numbered sections — project details, safeguards and stakeholder engagement, application of methodology, quantification, monitoring — plus two standing appendices, one for sensitive information and one for data and parameters. It is submitted as a non-editable PDF, and where the applied methodology has been digitalized, as the digital template in the Verra Project Hub instead.

Gold Standard's Project Design Document template v2.0 opens with a key project information block and a project impact summary, then runs sections A to I. The safeguarding assessment, the stakeholder consultation report and the SDG contributions are not an annex to the technical case; they sit inside the design document and are reviewed with it.

The practical consequence is ordering. Under VCS a developer can get a long way into methodology, quantification and monitoring before the social sections come due. Under Gold Standard the consultation has to have happened before the design document is finished, because the report of it is part of the document. That is a scheduling difference, not a paperwork one.

## What differs in consultation and public scrutiny?

Verra runs one public window. Under the [Registration and Issuance Process, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/), a project undergoes a 30-day public comment period that starts on the date its status becomes *under validation*, with comments submitted through the Verra Project Hub and a public summary posted at the end. Local stakeholder consultation is a requirement of the standard, but it is the proponent's to design and report.

Gold Standard prescribes the local process and adds its own public windows. The [Stakeholder Consultation Requirements, v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/102-par-stakeholder-consultation-requirements/), require one mandatory physical meeting — stakeholders invited at least 30 days beforehand, information shared in advance — and one stakeholder feedback round lasting at least one month. Then, during design review, Gold Standard itself runs a two-week public consultation on its Assurance platform, with the documentation also going to its Technical Advisory Committee and NGO Supporters; design review lasts a minimum of four weeks and the consultation sits inside it. The same two-week consultation recurs at performance review and at design certification renewal.

One deadline in that process is unforgiving. Where Gold Standard raises corrective action requests during design review, the developer and the VVB must respond within six weeks of receiving the comments; the [Principles & Requirements, v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/), state that a late submission results in the complete rejection of the request.

## What differs in the calendar and the cost?

Gold Standard's clock starts earliest: preliminary review has to be requested within one year of the project start date. Verra's v4.7 deadlines are two, five or eight years from the project start date depending on the project type, which gives a developer materially more room to assemble evidence before committing.

On registry fees the two are close enough that fees should not decide the choice — USD 1,500 plus USD 3,750 at Verra against USD 1,000 plus USD 2,500 at Gold Standard, with issuance levies of USD 0.23 and USD 0.25 per credit respectively. What differs more is what sits outside both schedules: the validation and verification body's audit fee, which neither registry sets and which is usually the largest single cost, and, for land use projects, the buffer. Verra withholds a share of credits set by an AFOLU risk rating between 12 and 60; Gold Standard withholds a flat 20% of credits issued to land use and forests projects. On a nature-based project that difference is worth more than every registry fee combined.

## Which labels can each registry put on a credit?

Both now carry the three labels buyers ask for: the ICVCM Core Carbon Principles label, a CORSIA label, and an Article 6 label for credits with host country authorization. So the label is rarely a reason to pick one registry over the other — but it is often a reason to check the methodology, because labels are awarded against methodologies and vintages, not against registries. A project should confirm that the specific methodology it intends to apply is eligible for the label its buyer needs before it lists anywhere.

For CORSIA in particular, credits of vintage 2021 or later need host country authorization under Article 6, plus either evidence of a corresponding adjustment or an approved insurance-backed guarantee. That is a government-facing workstream with its own timetable, and it is independent of which registry holds the project.

## How should a developer choose?

In the order the constraints actually bind:

1. **Is the project type eligible at all?** Gold Standard credits only carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide across five listed project types; the VCS scope is wider and includes activities Gold Standard does not take. If only one registry can take the activity, the decision is made.

2. **Is there an approved methodology that fits, and is it active?** A registry is only as useful as the methodology a project can actually apply, and applicability conditions are where most projects fail. Read them before choosing.

3. **Which deadline can the project still meet?** A project whose start date is already more than a year old has effectively lost the Gold Standard preliminary review window.

4. **What does the buyer need?** A specific label, a specific co-benefit story, or an SDG framing the buyer reports against.

5. **What can the team actually run?** Gold Standard's prescribed consultation and safeguarding process is more work up front and more certain in form; Verra's is more flexible and puts more of the design burden on the developer.

Fees and crediting-period length come last. They matter, but they rarely override the four questions above.

## How Climat handles this

Climat treats each registry as its own document with its own section list and its own order, rather than drafting one generic document and relabelling it. For VCS that is a ten-section list ending in the crediting period; for Gold Standard it is nine sections with safeguarding, consultation and SDG contributions near the front, where Gold Standard puts them. The methodology drives the intake questions and the applicability check either way.

What Climat cannot do is choose the registry for a developer. That decision rests on the project type, the methodology, the deadline already running, and what a buyer will pay for — and on evidence gathered outside any document. Climat's applicability check will tell a developer whether a methodology's conditions are met, not met, or need a person to look; the evidence gap report says what is still unproven. The choice of registry stays with the developer. See the [Verra VCS page](https://climat.today/registries/verra-vcs/) and the [Gold Standard page](https://climat.today/registries/gold-standard/) for each document section by section.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Verra or Gold Standard better for a carbon project?

Neither is better in general. Project type decides first, because Gold Standard credits only carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide and lists five project types, while the VCS scope is wider. After that the choice turns on the methodology available, the label the buyer needs, and the deadlines the project can still meet.

### Which version of the VCS rules applies to a project registering now?

It depends on the rule. Verra released VCS Version 5 on 16 December 2025, and most design rules take effect for requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027. The new stakeholder engagement and safeguard rules apply to projects with a start date on or after 1 January 2027. Earlier requests follow the VCS Standard, v4.7, unless the proponent opts into Version 5.

### How many Sustainable Development Goals must a project support?

Three under both registries. The VCS Standard requires contributions to at least three SDGs. Gold Standard requires positive impacts on at least three SDGs, one of which must be SDG 13, with monitoring indicators set in the Project Design Document.

### How long can a project earn credits under each registry?

Under the VCS Standard, v5.0, energy and industry projects get five years, renewable twice, and most land use projects get 20 to 100 years. Gold Standard certifies in five-year cycles, up to 15 years for renewable energy and community services projects and 30 to 50 years for afforestation and reforestation. VCS registration requests submitted before 1 January 2027 still use the v4.7 periods for energy and industry projects.

### What does it cost to register with Verra and with Gold Standard?

Verra charges USD 1,500 for pipeline listing and USD 3,750 for the registration review. Gold Standard charges USD 1,000 for preliminary review and USD 2,500 for design review. Both also charge account, verification and issuance fees, and neither schedule covers what the validation body charges for the audit.

### Can credits from both registries be used under CORSIA?

Yes, within the limits set by ICAO. Both registries label credits for the first phase, 2024 to 2026, and the second phase, 2027 to 2029. Credits of vintage 2021 or later need host country authorization under Article 6, plus either evidence of a corresponding adjustment or an approved insurance-backed guarantee.
