# What is a project design document (PDD)?

> A project design document (PDD) describes a carbon project and demonstrates that it meets the rules of a carbon standard and the applied methodology. The developer writes it, a validation/verification body audits it, and the registry publishes it. Verra calls it a project description; Gold Standard, the CDM and the Article 6.4 mechanism call it a PDD.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/guides/what-is-a-pdd/

- **Name under Verra VCS:** Project description
- **Name under Gold Standard, CDM and Article 6.4:** Project design document (PDD)
- **Current VCS templates:** v5.0A and v5.0B, issued 9 June 2026, required for project requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027
- **Current Gold Standard template:** Project Design Document template v2.0, 15 May 2026
- **Audited at:** Validation, by a validation/verification body
- **Companion document:** The monitoring report, prepared for each monitoring period and audited at verification

## What is a project design document?

A project design document (PDD) is the document in which a developer describes a carbon project and demonstrates that it meets the rules of a carbon standard and of the methodology it applies. It is written before validation, audited by a validation/verification body (VVB), and published by the registry.

The Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) defines the PDD in its [Glossary: CDM terms, version 11.0](https://cdm.unfccc.int/Reference/Guidclarif/glos_CDM.pdf) as the document prepared by the project participant that sets out in detail the project activity to be undertaken. Verra's [VCS Program Definitions v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-program-definitions-v5-0/) define the project description as the document that describes the project's GHG emission reduction or carbon dioxide removal activities and that uses Verra's template.

The document has three uses. It is the evidence a VVB assesses at validation. It fixes the baseline scenario, the additionality case, the estimated reductions or removals, and the monitoring plan. It is the reference for every later monitoring report and verification.

## What is the document called under each standard?

Verra calls it a project description. Gold Standard, the CDM and the Article 6.4 mechanism call it a project design document. The function is the same. The template and the section order are not.

| Standard | Name of the document | Template or form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verra Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) | Project description | [VCS Project Description Template v5.0A](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0a/) and [v5.0B](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0b/), issued 9 June 2026 |
| Gold Standard for the Global Goals | Project Design Document (PDD) | [Project Design Document template v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/t-prereview-design-document/), 15 May 2026 |
| Clean Development Mechanism | Project design document (PDD) | The PDD form published on the UNFCCC CDM website |
| Article 6.4 mechanism (Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism) | Project design document (PDD) | [PDD form for Article 6.4 projects](https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/A6.4-FORM-AC-020.pdf), A6.4-FORM-AC-020 version 02.0, 1 April 2026 |

Verra lists its current templates on the [VCS Program rules and requirements page](https://verra.org/programs/verified-carbon-standard/vcs-program-details/). Gold Standard lists its own on its [templates page](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/templates/). The Article 6.4 forms are listed on the Supervisory Body's [rules and regulations page](https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/bodies/constituted-bodies/article-64-supervisory-body/rules-and-regulations).

## Which VCS template applies, v5.0A or v5.0B?

The project start date decides. Verra released VCS Version 5 on 16 December 2025 and published two versions of each template on 9 June 2026.

| Template | Applies to | Rules reported against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| v5.0A | Projects with a start date before 1 January 2027 that submit a pipeline listing request, a registration request, or a crediting period renewal or baseline reassessment before 1 January 2030 | VCS Version 5, except that ownership, stakeholder engagement and safeguards follow sections 3.7, 3.18 and 3.19 of the VCS Standard v4.7 |
| v5.0B | Projects with a start date on or after 1 January 2027, and earlier projects at a crediting period renewal or baseline reassessment submitted on or after 1 January 2030 | VCS Version 5 in full, including sections 3.6, 3.17 and 3.18 of the VCS Standard v5.0 |

Verra's [release notice of 9 June 2026](https://verra.org/verra-operationalizes-vcs-version-5-with-publication-of-templates-and-guidance/) states that the v5.0 templates must be used for all project requests submitted after 1 January 2027, including projects whose audits are already underway. The [VCS Version 5 overview of updates and effective dates](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-version-5-overview-of-vcs-program-updates-and-effective-dates/) adds that a proponent who chooses to be validated to Version 5 before that date must use them too.

The previous template, v4.4 of April 2024, now sits on Verra's [Version 4 archive page](https://verra.org/programs/verified-carbon-standard/vcs-version-4-rules-and-requirements/), while Verra lists the VCS Standard v4.7 as active until 1 January 2027. For a request submitted before that date under v4.7, confirm with Verra or the VVB which template to use.

Section 3.4.1 of the [VCS Standard v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v5-0/) also provides for a digital project description template in the Verra Project Hub where the methodology has been digitalized. The June 2026 notice says digital versions of the Version 5 templates are still being built and that Verra will announce the date from which they become mandatory.

## What sections does a VCS project description contain?

Templates v5.0A and v5.0B each have five numbered sections and two standing appendices. The instructions inside the template are binding: section 3.4.1 of the VCS Standard v5.0 requires proponents to conform to all instructional text.

| Section | What it has to establish |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Project Details | What the project is, who the proponent is, where the project is, and that it is eligible: sectoral scope, start date, crediting period, scale, design, conditions before the project, legal compliance, and no double counting or double claiming. v5.0A covers ownership here. v5.0B covers the right to operate and the right to reductions and removals. |
| 2. Safeguards and Stakeholder Engagement | How stakeholders were consulted, whether free, prior and informed consent applies, how grievances are handled, and how risks to people and ecosystems are managed. v5.0B renames the section and draws on two standalone documents, the stakeholder engagement plan and the ESG risk assessment. |
| 3. Application of Methodology | That the methodology is active and applicable, with each [applicability condition](https://climat.today/guides/applicability-conditions/) justified separately. Then the project boundary, the baseline scenario, [additionality](https://climat.today/guides/additionality/) including regulatory surplus, and any methodology deviations. |
| 4. Quantification of Estimated Reductions and Removals | Baseline, project and leakage emissions, the non-permanence risk analysis and buffer allocation where relevant, and the estimated net reductions and removals. |
| 5. Monitoring | The data and parameters, and the monitoring plan: data collection and management, calibration, personnel, internal auditing and QA/QC, handling of non-conformances, and sampling. |
| Appendices | Sensitive information to be withheld from the public version, and the tables of data and parameters fixed at validation or monitored. |

## What sections does a Gold Standard PDD contain?

The Gold Standard PDD template v2.0 opens with key project information and a project impact summary, followed by lettered sections. The [Principles & Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/) require the PDD to carry the safeguarding assessment, the record of stakeholder consultation and the Monitoring & Reporting Plan.

| Section | What it has to establish |
| --- | --- |
| A. Project description | Location, technology or measures, funding structure, product ownership, eligibility, double counting risks, alignment with national climate and development policies, start date and crediting period. |
| B. Application of methodology(ies) | Applicability, project boundary, baseline scenario, additionality (prior consideration, regulatory surplus, financial additionality, common practice), risk of reversals, calculation of emission reductions or net removals, and the monitoring plan. |
| C. Safeguarding principles and gender sensitivity assessment | The risks identified against Gold Standard's safeguarding principles, with mitigation and monitoring. |
| D. Gender equality assessment | How the project meets the gender requirements, and the related monitoring. |
| E. Sustainable development contribution | The contribution to at least three Sustainable Development Goals, one of which must be SDG 13, and how each is monitored. |
| F. Stakeholder consultation assessment | Who was invited, how the consultation ran, the comments received, how they were considered, and the continuous input and grievance mechanism. |
| G to I | Contact information, appendices, and additional information for land use and forests projects. |

## Who writes the PDD and who reads it?

The developer writes it and answers for it. A VVB audits it. The registry reviews the audit and publishes the document.

- **Author.** Verra calls this party the project proponent and Gold Standard calls it the project developer. The [VCS Program Guide v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-program-guide-v5-0/) (section 2.6.1) makes the proponent responsible for providing the project description and supporting documentation.

- **Validation/verification body.** The VVB assesses the document against the standard and the methodology and issues a validation report. See [validation and verification](https://climat.today/guides/validation-and-verification/).

- **Registry.** Verra reviews each request to determine whether the VVB has appropriately assessed the project ([Registration and Issuance Process v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/), section 4.3). Gold Standard runs a design review in which the documents are open to its Technical Advisory Committee, its NGO supporters and the public.

- **The public.** Under section 3.4.7 of the VCS Standard v5.0, all information in project documents is presumed public. Gold Standard publishes project documentation on its Impact Registry, except confidential information.

## How does a PDD differ from a monitoring report?

The PDD is a forecast, written for validation. A monitoring report is a record, written for each monitoring period and audited at verification. Section 3.4 of the VCS Standard v5.0 says proponents prepare a project description for validation and a monitoring report for verification.

| Aspect | PDD or project description | Monitoring report |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When | Before validation | After each monitoring period |
| Figures | Estimated reductions and removals | Reductions and removals quantified from monitored data |
| Audit | Validation | Verification |
| Monitoring | Sets the monitoring plan | Reports results against that plan |
| Template | VCS Project Description Template, Gold Standard PDD template | [VCS Monitoring Report Template](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-monitoring-report-template-v5-0a/), [Gold Standard Monitoring Report template v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/t-perfcert-monitoring-report/) |

Under the VCS Standard v5.0 the monitoring report must state the reductions and removals generated in each calendar year of the monitoring period (section 3.4.3), and monitoring periods must not overlap (section 3.4.5).

## What causes validation findings on a PDD?

Neither Verra nor Gold Standard publishes a ranking of the most frequent findings. The standards do state what a VVB must raise, and the templates state what a compliant answer looks like. The causes below come from those texts.

- **Applicability conditions answered as a group.** The VCS template requires each condition to be justified separately, for every methodology, module and tool applied.

- **An inactive methodology version.** Under section 3.1.4 of the VCS Standard v5.0, the version applied must be active on the date the registration request is submitted.

- **An additionality analysis that cannot be reproduced.** The VCS template asks for enough data and parameters for a reader to reproduce the analysis and obtain the same results.

- **Sections deleted or marked "not applicable".** The VCS template requires an explanation and a justification instead.

- **Core information marked confidential.** Section 3.4.9 of the VCS Standard v5.0 bars proponents from withholding the baseline scenario, additionality, quantification, monitoring, or the non-permanence risk score.

- **Errors in the baseline, the parameters or the additionality assumptions.** Gold Standard's [Validation and Verification Standard v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/113-par-validation-and-verification-standard/) (paragraph 6.3.14) names these as grounds for a corrective action request, together with non-compliance in stakeholder consultation, safeguarding or the sustainable development assessment.

- **Weak technical detail.** Verra's [Validation and Verification Manual v3.2](https://verra.org/documents/validation-and-verification-manual-v3-2/) (section 3.4) lists four common sources of material error: incomplete identification of GHG sources, sinks and reservoirs; calibration; emission factors, units and conversion factors; and models.

Whether a given gap becomes a finding is the VVB's judgment. The manual dates from 2016 and is guidance, not a rule, but section 4.1.8 of the VCS Standard v5.0 expects VVBs to follow it.

## How Climat handles this

Climat [drafts each section](https://climat.today/product/document-drafting/) of the registry's project document in the registry's own order: the VCS project description or the Gold Standard for the Global Goals PDD. Statements carry citations to the intake data, to excerpts of the uploaded evidence, or to the methodology, and every section is reviewed, edited and finalized by a person. Climat is not a registry and not a validation body, and it does not replace validation or verification.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a VCS project description the same thing as a PDD?

In function, yes. Verra's VCS Program uses the term project description for the document that Gold Standard, the CDM and the Article 6.4 mechanism call a project design document. Each one describes the project, the baseline, additionality, the estimated reductions and the monitoring plan, and each is audited at validation. The template and the section order differ by standard.

### Which VCS project description template should I use, v5.0A or v5.0B?

Use v5.0A if the project start date is before 1 January 2027 and v5.0B if it is on or after that date. Verra requires the v5.0 templates for all project requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027. A project that starts on v5.0A moves to v5.0B at a crediting period renewal or baseline reassessment submitted on or after 1 January 2030.

### Who is responsible for what a PDD says?

The project proponent under Verra, or the project developer under Gold Standard, even when a consultant writes the text. The validation/verification body assesses the document and does not write it. Under the VCS Standard v5.0, the validation opinion must state that the GHG statement is the responsibility of the project proponent.

### Is the PDD made public?

Yes. Under the VCS Standard v5.0 all information in project documents is presumed public, and only information that meets Verra's definition of commercially sensitive information may be withheld. The baseline scenario, additionality, quantification, monitoring and the non-permanence risk score can never be withheld. Gold Standard publishes project documentation on its Impact Registry, except confidential information.

### Can the PDD be changed after validation?

Yes, through a formal route. Under the VCS Standard v5.0 a change is a project description deviation, which must be described and is assessed by a validation/verification body at the next verification. Gold Standard handles changes to a design certified project through its design change request procedure, which its Principles & Requirements v2.1 reference in Annex A.

### Does a PDD have to be written in English?

Under Verra, yes: the VCS Standard v5.0 requires project documents to be in English. Gold Standard requires English or another language agreed between the project developer, Gold Standard and the validation/verification body.

# Methodologies

> A methodology is the rulebook a carbon project is assessed against. For each methodology Climat supports, these pages explain what it covers, which conditions a project must meet, how additionality and the baseline are established, and what has to be monitored. Every page names the version it describes and the date it was checked.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/methodologies/

## How does Climat add a methodology?

We read the published methodology in full, then write down its applicability conditions, the inputs it requires, its approach to additionality, its baseline, and its monitoring parameters. Anything we could not check against the primary text is marked as unverified and is not offered to customers.

That is why the list is short. A methodology that is nearly right produces a project document that is nearly right, and a validator will find the difference.

## Which methodology should we add next?

The order is set by the people using Climat. If you are working under a methodology that is not listed here, [tell us which one](https://climat.today/contact/) and where your project stands.

# VM0047 explained: applicability, additionality, baseline and monitoring

> VM0047 is Verra's methodology for afforestation, reforestation and revegetation. Version 1.1, active since 14 May 2025, credits carbon dioxide removals under two mutually exclusive approaches: an area-based approach that uses a remote-sensing performance benchmark, and a census-based approach for dispersed planting of up to 50 planting units per hectare with a zero baseline.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/methodologies/vm0047/

- **Code:** VM0047
- **Current version:** 1.1, issued 14 May 2025
- **Status:** Active on Verra's methodology page
- **Sectoral scope:** 14, Forestry and other land use (forests, wetlands, and grasslands)
- **Approach:** Area-based (performance method) or census-based (project method); removals only
- **Governing registry:** Verra, Verified Carbon Standard (VCS)
- **Last checked:** 29 September 2026

## What does VM0047 cover, and which version is current?

VM0047 quantifies carbon dioxide removals from afforestation, reforestation and revegetation (ARR) under Verra's Verified Carbon Standard. The current version is [VM0047 v1.1](https://verra.org/documents/vm0047-afforestation-reforestation-and-revegetation-v1-1/), issued on 14 May 2025. [Verra's methodology page](https://verra.org/methodologies/vm0047-afforestation-reforestation-and-revegetation-v1-1/) listed it as active, under sectoral scope 14, when checked on 29 September 2026.

Version 1.0 is closed to new projects. The same page sets a grace period: projects using v1.0 had to request pipeline listing as under validation by 31 December 2025 and must request registration by 31 December 2026.

## What is the difference between the area-based and census-based approaches?

The area-based approach measures carbon per hectare and credits only growth beyond a benchmark observed on control plots. The census-based approach counts individual planting units against a zero baseline. The two are mutually exclusive for a project activity instance, and the choice made at the project start date holds for the whole crediting period (Section 4.1).

| Feature | Area-based | Census-based |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where it fits | Non-forest becomes forest, or stocks rise in forest not managed for wood products in the past ten years | Planting outside forest that does not change land use |
| Scaling | Plot sampling per hectare, multiplied by project area | Sampled planting units, multiplied by the census count and adjusted for mortality |
| Baseline | Dynamic performance benchmark | Zero |
| Additionality | Regulatory surplus, performance benchmark, investment analysis | Regulatory surplus, investment analysis, common practice |
| Carbon pools | Woody biomass, plus other pools the project significantly reduces | Woody biomass only |
| Leakage | Quantified with VMD0054 | Set to zero |

## Which project activities are eligible, and which are excluded?

Eligible activities establish, increase or restore vegetative cover by direct planting, seeding or assisted natural regeneration (Section 4). Section 4.4 lists exclusions and describes the list as non-exhaustive:

- **Area-based:** land that met the definition of managed forest at any point in the 10 years before the project start date; clearing of pre-existing woody biomass that involves timber harvesting or degrades native ecosystems; planting below 50 units per hectare that could use the census-based approach.

- **Census-based:** sites where woody biomass serving a similar purpose to the planting units was removed in the last 10 years; soil inversion deeper than 25 cm.

## What are the applicability conditions of VM0047?

Every project meets the five general conditions, then all conditions of the approach it applies. The table paraphrases Section 4 of version 1.1.

| Section | Condition | Plain-language reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4.1(1) | Project activities increase vegetative cover. | The project adds vegetation that can be measured. |
| 4.1(2) | Where both approaches are used, they cover non-overlapping areas defined at the project start. | Map every parcel to one approach before the start date. |
| 4.1(3) | The approach chosen at the start date applies for the whole crediting period. | No switching later. |
| 4.1(4) | The start date is the earlier of the start of site preparation and the land use change date. | Keep dated evidence of whichever came first. |
| 4.1(5) | On organic soils or wetlands, VM0047 covers aboveground biomass and a wetland methodology covers other pools. | VM0047 alone is not enough on peat or wetland. |
| 4.2(1) | Area-based: direct planting, indirect measures of assisted natural regeneration, or both. | Seeding, weed control and grazing barriers qualify. |
| 4.2(2) | Area-based: a carbon stock estimate at t = 0 exists for every significant pool, within two years of the start date. | Measure plots before clearing. A disturbed pool with no t = 0 measurement makes the project ineligible. |
| 4.2(3) | Area-based: leakage is quantified with VMD0054, never assumed de minimis. | A leakage calculation is mandatory. |
| 4.3(1) | Census-based: direct planting only. | No assisted natural regeneration. |
| 4.3(2) | Pre-project land use continues for the project lifetime. | On farmland, farming goes on. |
| 4.3(3) | At most 50 planting units per hectare, scaled to instance size and dispersed. | Half a hectare allows 25 units. |
| 4.3(4) | A complete census of units planted by the proponent marks t = 0. | Existing trees are outside the census and the density limit. |
| 4.3(5) | Dead units may be replanted within the 50 per hectare limit. | Replanting cannot raise the ceiling. |
| 4.3(6) | Each unit is identified by a GPS point, spaced at least the GPS accuracy apart, or by a durable marker with a unique ID. | With 5 m accuracy, units stand at least 5 m apart. |
| 4.3(7) | A unit that cannot be located at monitoring is assumed dead. | Lost records cost credits. |
| 4.3(8) | The area has under 10% pre-existing woody biomass cover, and/or is continuously cropped or classed as settlements or other lands. | See the note below. |
| 4.3(9) | Project soil disturbance occurs only at planting. Soil inversion stays within 25 cm and happens once per crediting period. | Pit planting may go deeper than 25 cm. |

Two points of wording need care. Section 4.3(8) joins its limbs with "and/or", while Section 6.2 requires both before the baseline is set to zero. Section 4.1(4) dates the project start from site preparation or land use change, while Section 4.3(4) says the census marks the start. Settle both readings with the validation body.

## How is additionality demonstrated under VM0047?

Area-based projects use a performance method and census-based projects a project method (Section 7). Both show regulatory surplus under the VCS Program rules.

- **Performance benchmark (area-based).** The stocking index trend on project plots must differ significantly from the trend on matched control plots: a Z value of 1.96 or more in absolute terms. It is shown ex ante at validation and retested at each verification.

- **Investment analysis.** Benchmark or investment comparison analysis under Step 3 of [VT0008](https://verra.org/documents/vt0008-additionality-assessment-v1-0/). Census-based projects always need it. Area-based projects skip it only where they have no revenue or incentive other than carbon credit sales.

- **Common practice (census-based).** Similar landowners are surveyed within five years of the start date. Adoption below 15% among landowners without carbon finance means the activity is not common practice. At 15% or above the project is not additional (Section 7.3.4).

## How is the baseline set?

The area-based baseline is the performance benchmark: the ratio of the stocking index trend on control plots to the trend on project plots (Appendix 1). At least 30 project plots of 0.01 to 10 hectares are sampled. Control plots share the jurisdiction, ecoregion, policy environment and land tenure class, lie within 100 km at first, and are matched on ten years of stocking index history. Where the trends do not differ significantly, the benchmark is set to 1.

The census-based baseline is zero where the site has under 10% pre-existing woody biomass cover and is continuously cropped or classed as settlements or other lands (Section 6.2). Continuous cropping means cultivation of the same site every year for 10 years or more, with no fallow longer than one season.

## How are removals quantified?

Both approaches use stock difference: stock at this monitoring event minus stock at the previous one, net of uncertainty and project emissions (Section 8.6). Area-based projects also deduct the benchmark and leakage.

Census-based, Equation 33: `CR_t = ΔC_WP,t × (1 − UNC_t) − ΔC_WP,t−x × (1 − UNC_t−x) − PE_t`

| Parameter | Meaning | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `N` | Planting units at the initial census | Complete census |
| `M_t` | Mortality through year t | Re-enumeration or sampling |
| `B_WP-woody-AB,pu,t` | Aboveground woody biomass of a sampled unit | Field measurement, allometric equations |
| `R`, `CF` | Root-to-shoot ratio, carbon fraction | Project-specific; 0.47 |
| `PB_t` | Performance benchmark | Appendix 1 |
| `UNC_t` | Uncertainty deduction at 90% confidence | Equations 28 and 29 |
| `PE_t` | Emissions from biomass burning and nitrogen fertilizer | Sections 8.2.2 and 8.3.2 |

No removals are credited where the half-width of the 90% confidence interval exceeds 100% of the estimate (Section 8.5).

## What must be monitored, and how often?

Field parameters are monitored every five years or more frequently, and the stocking index at least annually (Section 9.2 and Appendix 1).

| Parameter | Approach | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Woody biomass, and other included biomass pools, on plots | Area-based | Every five years or more frequently |
| Soil organic carbon, where included | Area-based | At t = 0 and each verification, with limited exceptions |
| Stocking index, project and control plots | Area-based | At least annually |
| Mortality, biomass of sampled units, sampled units burned | Census-based | Every five years or more frequently |
| Fertilizer mass and nitrogen content | Both | At least every five years, or before each verification if more frequent |

## Which tools and modules does VM0047 call on?

- [VMD0054](https://verra.org/methodologies/vmd0054-estimating-leakage-from-the-displacement-of-agricultural-activities-v1-1/), the leakage module, in its most recent version. Verra lists v1.1 as active since 13 January 2026.

- VT0008 Additionality Assessment, Step 3.

- The [VCS Standard](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v5-0/), for the long-term average where the project harvests and for the non-permanence risk report (Section 3.2.11). See the [Verra VCS page](https://climat.today/registries/verra-vcs/).

## What is commonly challenged at validation?

This list is not based on validation statistics. It collects the points where the methodology demands evidence or leaves room for judgment.

- **Start date and t = 0.** Dated evidence, and plot measurements inside the two-year windows.

- **Land history.** Photos or attestations that no similar woody biomass was removed in 10 years.

- **Common practice.** Whether the sample is representative and the geographic domain is drawn correctly.

- **Allometric equations.** Global equations must rest on destructive sampling from the same ecoregion or Holdridge life zone.

- **Census records.** Unique ID, geo-referenced point, planting year and species for every unit.

## How Climat handles this

Climat supports VM0047 v1.1 under the census-based approach. The intake form is generated from the inputs the methodology requires, and the [applicability check](https://climat.today/product/applicability-check/) evaluates every applicability condition as pass, fail or needs review, routing conditions that call for judgment to a person. Climat is not a registry and not a validation body.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I use the VM0047 census-based approach for assisted natural regeneration?

No. The census-based approach covers direct planting only (Section 4.3). Assisted natural regeneration is eligible under the area-based approach, which requires a performance benchmark built from matched control plots and a leakage calculation under VMD0054.

### What is the maximum planting density under the VM0047 census-based approach?

Fifty planting units per hectare, scaled to the size of each instance, so a half-hectare instance may hold 25 units. In larger instances planting has to be dispersed, not concentrated in one part. Existing vegetation does not count toward the limit.

### Does a census-based VM0047 project have to quantify leakage?

No. Leakage is set to zero under the census-based approach, because the pre-project land use has to continue and planting density is capped (Section 8.4). Area-based projects must quantify leakage with module VMD0054 and may not assume it is de minimis.

### How often does VM0047 require biomass to be measured?

Field parameters such as biomass and mortality are monitored every five years or more frequently. Under the area-based approach the stocking index of project and control plots is recorded at least annually. The performance benchmark is updated at each verification or every five years, whichever comes first.

### Can a project still use VM0047 version 1.0?

Only a project that was already in the pipeline. Verra's grace period required projects using version 1.0 to request pipeline listing as under validation by 31 December 2025, and they must request registration by 31 December 2026. All other projects apply version 1.1.

### Which carbon pools does VM0047 count?

The census-based approach counts aboveground and belowground woody biomass only and excludes every other pool as conservative. The area-based approach always counts woody biomass. It adds non-woody biomass, dead wood, litter and soil organic carbon where the project significantly reduces them, tested with Appendix 2 of the methodology.

2. [VM0047 methodology page: status, sectoral scope and grace periods](https://verra.org/methodologies/vm0047-afforestation-reforestation-and-revegetation-v1-1/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)
3. [VMD0054 Estimating Leakage from the Displacement of Agricultural Activities, v1.1, module page](https://verra.org/methodologies/vmd0054-estimating-leakage-from-the-displacement-of-agricultural-activities-v1-1/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)
4. [VT0008 Additionality Assessment, v1.0 (14 October 2024)](https://verra.org/documents/vt0008-additionality-assessment-v1-0/), Verra (accessed 2026-09-29)

# VMR0017 explained: eligibility, additionality, baseline and monitoring

> VMR0017 Grid-Connected Electricity Generation from Renewable Sources (ACM0002 Revision) is a Verra methodology revision, version 1.0 of 23 April 2026. It cannot be used on its own: the procedures of CDM methodology ACM0002, v22.0, apply except where VMR0017 replaces them. It sets eligibility through a technology, capacity and geography table, replaces four CDM tools with VCS tools, adds project emissions from battery fire suppression agents, and treats the plant's embodied emissions as leakage.

Updated 2026-09-30. Canonical: https://climat.today/methodologies/vmr0017/

- **Code:** VMR0017, a revision of CDM methodology ACM0002
- **Current version:** 1.0, issued 23 April 2026
- **Sectoral scope:** 1, Energy supply
- **Applied with:** ACM0002, v22.0 — VMR0017 is not a standalone methodology
- **Approach:** Project method for both additionality and the crediting baseline; reductions, not removals
- **Additionality:** VT0008 — regulatory surplus, investment analysis, common practice; barrier analysis not applicable
- **Last checked:** 30 September 2026

## What does VMR0017 cover, and how does it relate to ACM0002?

VMR0017 is a *methodology revision*, not a methodology. Verra developed version 1.0, issued 23 April 2026, on top of the Clean Development Mechanism methodology [ACM0002 Grid-connected Electricity Generation from Renewable Sources, v22.0](https://verra.org/documents/vmr0017-grid-connected-electricity-generation-from-renewable-sources/), and states plainly that it must be used with ACM0002, v22.0. The procedures and requirements of ACM0002 apply unless VMR0017 says otherwise (Section 2). Everything below is what VMR0017 adds or replaces; the rest of a project's quantification still comes out of ACM0002.

The revision does five things. It widens geographic eligibility through a new table of technologies, capacities and geographies. It replaces four CDM tools with VCS tools. It adds provisions for battery energy storage systems, both for grid charging and for the release of fire suppression agents. It makes the power plant's embodied emissions a leakage term, where ACM0002 largely had none. And it removes the simplified additionality procedure that relied on a CDM positive-list tool.

Its summary table sets the three things a Verra methodology has to declare: additionality is established by a **project method**, the crediting baseline is a **project method**, and the mitigation outcome is **reductions** — not removals. A project under VMR0017 therefore argues its own case rather than being deemed additional by a positive list, and it generates avoided emissions rather than carbon removals.

## Which projects are eligible?

All applicability conditions in Section 2.2 of ACM0002 have to be met, with replacements. The important one is condition 8(a), which VMR0017 rewrites so that a project activity must correspond to one or more rows of its own Table 1. That table is the heart of the revision, because it is where geography enters.

| Technology | Capacity | Geographies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wind (onshore and offshore), geothermal, terrestrial solar PV | Any | Low-, lower-middle- and upper-middle-income countries only, by World Bank country and lending group |
| Floating solar, wave, tidal | Any | Globally applicable |
| Hydroelectric | 15 MW or less, taken as the higher of the rated capacity and the authorized capacity named in the activity approval from the regulator or government | Least developed countries only, by the UN list |

Two notes attached to the table matter as much as the table. Projects and instances already registered under ACM0002 or AMS-I.D. Grid-connected Renewable Electricity Generation keep their original maximum crediting period, but every *new* project activity instance has to correspond to a row above. And this applicability condition supersedes the default eligibility for project activities given in the VCS Standard — so a technology that the VCS Standard would otherwise admit is still out of scope here if Table 1 does not list it.

VMR0017 also adds condition 8(f) for projects that integrate a battery. The battery and the power plant must be on the same site, directly connected to each other, and share a common grid connection — VMR0017's footnote defines that as feeding into or drawing from the grid through a single grid connection or metering point. Both facilities must be owned and operated by the same entity and be part of the same investment decision. Finally, replaced condition 14 pulls in the applicability conditions of every tool the revision calls on, so VT0008 and VT0011 each add their own gate.

Because eligibility turns on a country's World Bank income classification and the UN list of least developed countries, it can change over a project's life. Both lists are revised periodically, and Table 1 points at the live lists rather than a snapshot.

## Which CDM tools does VMR0017 replace?

Section 2 makes four substitutions that a developer has to carry through every reference in ACM0002:

| CDM tool in ACM0002 | VCS tool to use instead |
| --- | --- |
| TOOL01 Tool for the Demonstration and Assessment of Additionality | [VT0008 Additionality Assessment](https://verra.org/documents/vt0008-additionality-assessment-v1-0/) |
| TOOL02 Combined Tool to Identify the Baseline Scenario and Demonstrate Additionality | VT0009 Combined Baseline and Additionality Assessment |
| TOOL05 Baseline, Project and/or Leakage Emissions from Electricity Consumption and Monitoring of Electricity Generation | VT0010 Emissions from Electricity Consumption and Generation |
| TOOL07 Tool to Calculate the Emission Factor for an Electricity System | [VT0011 Electricity System Emission Factors](https://verra.org/documents/vt0011-electricity-system-emission-factors-v1-0/) |

A fifth tool is simply gone. VMR0017 records that CDM TOOL32 Positive Lists of Technologies was inactivated under the VCS Program on 1 October 2025 and is not eligible under the revision. That is why Section 7 deletes ACM0002's paragraph 35, the simplified procedure to demonstrate additionality: there is no positive list to fall back on.

## How is additionality demonstrated?

VMR0017 replaces ACM0002's additionality paragraph with a three-step demonstration built on VT0008:

1. **Regulatory surplus**, in accordance with the applicable version of the VCS Standard. Under [VCS Program Definitions, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-program-definitions-v5-0/), that means the activity is not mandated by any law or regulatory framework in a high-income country, and not mandated by a systematically enforced one elsewhere.

2. **Investment analysis**, following Step 3 of VT0008. Where the project applies benchmark analysis, the project documents must record whether the demonstration followed Sections 5.4.2(2)(b) and (c) of VT0008.

3. **Common practice**, following Step 4 of VT0008.

A note then removes an option that grid renewable projects have historically leaned on: barrier analysis, Step 2 of VT0008, is not applicable under VMR0017. The financial case has to carry the argument. Our [guide to additionality](https://climat.today/guides/additionality/) sets out what Step 3 and Step 4 of VT0008 each ask for, including the factor-F threshold that decides common practice.

## How is the baseline scenario identified?

For a greenfield plant, ACM0002's baseline is unchanged: the electricity the project supplies would otherwise have come from the grid, and the grid's emission factor does the work. VMR0017 rewrites the baseline procedure only for *retrofit, rehabilitation or replacement of an existing power plant*, where the counterfactual is genuinely contested.

There, Step 1 applies Step 1 of VT0009 and the alternatives must include three named scenarios: P1, the project activity undertaken without registration under a GHG program; P2, continuation of the current situation, using the equipment already in use with business-as-usual maintenance, with the extra power coming from existing and new grid-connected plants; and P3, all other plausible, technically feasible alternatives that increase generation at the site, including different levels of replacement, retrofit or rehabilitation, limited to alternatives actually available to the proponent.

Step 3 then routes the investment analysis by which scenarios survive: an investment comparison analysis under Step 3 of VT0009 where more than one alternative remains and those include P1 and P3, or a benchmark analysis under Step 3 (Option 2) of VT0008 where the remaining alternatives include P1 and P2.

## How are reductions quantified?

Net reductions follow the familiar form, with leakage no longer optional:

`ER(y) = BE(y) - PE(y) - LE(y)`

Baseline emissions are unchanged from ACM0002 — generation supplied to the grid multiplied by the combined margin grid emission factor, which under the revision is calculated with VT0011 rather than TOOL07. VT0011 sets the operating margin, build margin and combined margin procedures, and VMR0017 lets the proponent select the ex-ante or the ex-post option for the combined margin, provided the project documents record which was used, referencing paragraph 72(b) of VT0011 and paragraph 42(b) of TOOL07.

Project emissions are usually zero for renewable generation, but VMR0017 expands the equation to six terms: fossil fuel consumption, geothermal plant operation, hydropower and pumped-storage reservoirs, charging a battery from the grid or from fossil generators, grid electricity used for pumped-storage pumping beyond the paired renewable plant's output, and the release of fire suppression agents. The reservoir default emission factor is fixed at 100 kg CO 2 e/MWh, sourced from the Hydropower Sustainability Standard and its guidelines on good international industry practice.

### Battery fire suppression agents

This is new. VMR0017 states that projects should use low- or zero-GWP agents such as Novec 1230, where "low" means a global warming potential below 1. Where an agent with a GWP above 1 is used — HFC-227ea is the example given — the emissions are the mass released in each event multiplied by the agent's 100-year GWP. The GWP comes from the IPCC AR5 values as published by the GHG Protocol; for commercial blends it comes from manufacturer specifications, or a weighted average of the constituents, and where an agent is not listed, from a national or international regulatory authority such as the US EPA, or failing that from peer-reviewed literature.

### Embodied emissions as leakage

VMR0017 replaces ACM0002's Section 5.6 outright. Leakage is the life-cycle emissions of the plant — construction, operation and decommissioning, dominated in the literature by transport of equipment, people and expendables to the site and to upstream manufacturing — annualised by net generation. For a greenfield plant, leakage is net generation supplied to the grid multiplied by a technology emission factor; for a capacity addition, the generation added under the project activity is used instead.

| Renewable generation technology | Embodied emission factor (g CO 2 e/kWh) |
| --- | --- |
| Solar photovoltaic | 43 |
| Wind (onshore and offshore) | 13 |
| Biomass | 52 |
| Geothermal | 37 |
| Hydropower | 21 |
| Ocean energy | 8 |
| Concentrating solar power (tower and trough) | 28 |

The values come from NREL's *Life Cycle Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Electricity Generation: Update* of September 2021. For a technology not in the table, the proponent may take a value from credible and reputable sources or literature, but must justify the choice and document its source in the project documents.

## What must be monitored, and how often?

The parameter that drives everything is net electricity supplied to the grid — `EG(facility,y)` for the plant, or `EG(PJ_Add,y)` for generation added under the project. VMR0017 requires **direct measurement** with electricity meters installed at the grid interface for export, monitored continuously and aggregated at least monthly.

The QA/QC requirements are specific. Meters are tested and calibrated per utility or national requirements and manufacturer specifications, and cross-checked against utility or supplier receipts and invoices where applicable. Uncertainty is propagated per ACM0002 and VMR0017: for direct measurement, the actual metering uncertainty from the last calibration event, or the manufacturer's figure where no previous calibration exists; for estimates, zero where the estimate is conservative and a project-specific uncertainty where it is statistically significant. Cumulative meters are read as the difference between initial and final readings with both dates recorded, and linear interpolation is used where reading dates do not line up with the monitoring period. Where historical data feed the baseline, the proponent uses at least three years of the most recent records, or justifies why older data or a shorter period is more appropriate.

There is a narrow escape hatch: where direct measurement is temporarily not feasible for technical or logistical reasons — no access to monitoring equipment, maintenance, a remote or hazardous location — estimation methods in line with VT0010 may be used, with a justification, a demonstration that the constraint is temporary, and a demonstration that the estimation method is conservative.

Two further parameters are monitored where they apply: the mass of fire suppression agent released per event, and the electricity drawn from the grid by a battery or a pumped-storage plant, both handled through VT0010.

## Where the evidence has to be strongest

These are the places where VMR0017's own text, rather than any general practice, puts the burden on the developer — and where the [Validation and Verification Manual, v3.2](https://verra.org/documents/validation-and-verification-manual-v3-2/), requires the validation and verification body to test the evidence rather than accept the assertion:

- **The Table 1 row.** Eligibility is not "renewable energy"; it is a technology, a capacity and a geography in combination. A hydro project has to evidence both the LDC listing and the higher of rated and authorized capacity, with the activity approval on file.

- **The investment analysis.** With barrier analysis removed, Step 3 of VT0008 is the whole additionality case, and a benchmark analysis carries an explicit documentation requirement about how it was performed.

- **Common practice.** Step 4 of VT0008 needs a defensible population of similar projects and a reasoned account of which distinctions are essential.

- **The grid emission factor.** VT0011 offers several operating-margin methods and an ex-ante or ex-post combined margin; the choice has to be recorded and the data behind it has to be traceable.

- **Battery integration.** Condition 8(f) is five separate facts — same site, direct connection, common grid connection, same owner and operator, same investment decision — and each needs a document behind it.

- **Metering.** Calibration records and the uncertainty figure drawn from them, not just the meter readings.

## How Climat handles this

Climat seeds VMR0017's inputs as a methodology in the same way as VM0047, so the intake asks for the technology type, the installed capacity, the host country, whether the plant is grid connected, whether a battery is integrated and which grid emission factor option is being used. The rule-based applicability pass returns pass, fail or needs review against each condition, and the matrix conditions — the Table 1 combination, and condition 8(f) — return *needs review* rather than a verdict, because they are judgments a person has to make on documents. The evidence gap report then lists what is still unproven, most serious first, before drafting starts, and drafted sections carry citations to the intake data, to excerpts of the evidence supplied, or to the methodology. Climat does not validate a project and is not a registry.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a hydropower project use VMR0017?

Only in a least developed country, and only at 15 MW or less. Table 1 of the revised applicability condition lists hydroelectric for LDCs alone, with capacity taken as the higher of the rated capacity and the authorized capacity named in the activity approval. Wind, geothermal and terrestrial solar PV are eligible at any capacity but only in low-, lower-middle- and upper-middle-income countries. Floating solar, wave and tidal are globally applicable at any capacity.

### Do I have to demonstrate a barrier under VMR0017?

No. VMR0017 states that barrier analysis, Step 2 of VT0008, is not applicable. Additionality is three steps: regulatory surplus under the applicable version of the VCS Standard, an investment analysis under Step 3 of VT0008, and a common practice assessment under Step 4. A project applying benchmark analysis must also record in the project documents whether the demonstration followed Sections 5.4.2(2)(b) and (c) of VT0008.

### Is leakage zero for a grid-connected renewable energy project?

Not under VMR0017. It replaces ACM0002's leakage section with the plant's embodied emissions — construction, operation and decommissioning, parameterised on net generation supplied to the grid. Leakage is net generation in the year multiplied by a technology default emission factor from NREL's life-cycle update: 43 g CO2e/kWh for solar photovoltaic, 13 for wind, 21 for hydropower, 37 for geothermal, 52 for biomass, 28 for concentrating solar power and 8 for ocean energy.

### What does VMR0017 require of a project that includes battery storage?

Added applicability condition 8(f) requires the battery energy storage system and the power plant to be on the same site, directly connected to each other, sharing a common grid connection, owned and operated by the same entity and part of the same investment decision. Charging the battery from the grid or from fossil generators is a project emission, calculated under Scenario A of VT0010. Where a fire suppression agent with a global warming potential above 1 is used, the mass released multiplied by the agent's GWP is also a project emission.

### Which CDM tools does VMR0017 replace?

Four. TOOL01 is replaced by VT0008 Additionality Assessment, TOOL02 by VT0009 Combined Baseline and Additionality Assessment, TOOL05 by VT0010 Emissions from Electricity Consumption and Generation, and TOOL07 by VT0011 Electricity System Emission Factors. CDM TOOL32 Positive Lists of Technologies was inactivated under the VCS Program on 1 October 2025 and is not eligible, so ACM0002's simplified additionality procedure is removed.

### How long can a VMR0017 project be credited for?

Energy and industry projects sit in the five-year row of Table 8 of the VCS Standard, v5.0: a five-year crediting period, renewable twice, to a maximum total of 15 years, for registration requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027. Projects and instances already registered under ACM0002 or AMS-I.D. keep their original maximum crediting period, but every new project activity instance has to correspond to a row of VMR0017's Table 1.

# How Climat works: from methodology choice to export

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/product/

Product

One workspace, from methodology choice to a finished project document.

Climat takes a carbon project through seven steps: choose the registry and methodology, complete an intake built from that methodology, upload evidence, check applicability, review the evidence gaps, draft each section with citations, then review, finalize and export. A person decides at every step.

## What happens at each step?

Each step produces something you can read and check before the next one starts.

| Step | You provide | Climat does | You get |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Registry and methodology | Your choice of registry, sector and methodology | Loads the document structure of the registry and the requirements of the methodology | An intake form with only the inputs this methodology needs |
| 2. Intake and evidence | Answers to the intake, and evidence as PDF, Word or text | Extracts the text of each file and flags any file it cannot read | A record of what was supplied and what could not be used |
| 3. Applicability | Nothing further | Evaluates every applicability condition against your inputs | Pass, fail or needs review for each condition |
| 4. Evidence gaps | Nothing further | Compares what the case needs with what you supplied | A list of gaps: blocking, required and advisory |
| 5. Drafting | A decision to start | Drafts each section in the registry's order, with citations and warnings | A complete first draft you can trace |
| 6. Review | Your edits and instructions | Rewrites a section on request and keeps finalized sections untouched | Sections finalized by a person |
| 7. Export | A decision to finalize | Assembles the case and writes the cover note | One document, with AI assistance disclosed |

## What does each part do?

- [Available Applicability check Every condition of the methodology, evaluated as pass, fail or needs review. Read →](https://climat.today/product/applicability-check/)

- [Available Document drafting Each section of the project document, with a citation on every claim. Read →](https://climat.today/product/document-drafting/)

- [In development Pre-validation review An adversarial read of the finished draft, before the validator reads it. Read →](https://climat.today/product/pre-validation/)

- [In development Monitoring periods The methodology's monitoring parameters, tracked period by period. Read →](https://climat.today/product/monitoring/)

## What do you have at the end?

### The project document

Every section the registry requires, in the registry's order, each one finalized by a person on your team.

### A trail for every claim

Citations on the statements in the draft. Any citation that could not be matched to the evidence you supplied is flagged, not hidden.

### A cover note

A note for the validation and verification body that states plainly that AI assistance was used in preparing the document.

## What will Climat not do?

The limits are part of the product.

### It will not invent evidence

Where a document is missing, the draft says evidence is needed. It does not supply a plausible number.

### It will not decide for you

Conditions that need judgment are routed to a person. Sections are final only when a person finalizes them.

### It will not replace validation

Climat is not a registry and not a validation body. It does not guarantee registration, and it does not submit on your behalf.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I edit what Climat drafts?

Yes. Every section can be edited by hand, or rewritten by giving Climat your own instructions. Nothing is final until a person finalizes it, and a finalized section is never regenerated.

### What happens when the evidence for a claim is missing?

The evidence gap report lists it before drafting starts. If drafting goes ahead without it, the section says that evidence is needed instead of stating a figure that nothing supports.

### Can Climat draft for a methodology that is not listed?

No. Climat drafts only for methodologies that have been set up from the published methodology text. Today that is Verra VM0047 version 1.1, census-based approach, and Verra VMR0017 version 1.0. Tell us which methodology you need.

### Does Climat submit the project to the registry?

No. Climat prepares the document. Submission to the validation and verification body and to the registry stays with the project proponent.

# Applicability check

> The applicability check evaluates every applicability condition of the chosen methodology against the project's intake and returns one of three results for each: pass, fail, or needs review. It is rule-based, not generated, and a condition that calls for judgment is sent to a person instead of being guessed.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/product/applicability-check/

## What does the applicability check do?

It takes the applicability conditions of the methodology you chose and tests your project against each one. Nothing is skipped: a methodology with nine conditions produces nine results.

The check runs as soon as the intake is submitted, before any drafting. If the methodology does not fit, you find out before you have spent time on a document.

Applicability checkVM0047 v1.1

- Planting density does not exceed 50 planting units per hectare Intake: 45 units per hectare Pass

- No similar-purpose woody biomass removed from the area in the last 10 years Intake: none removed. Land records uploaded. Pass

- Soil inversion stays within the methodology's depth limit Not yet answered in the intake Needs review

Illustrative example showing three of the methodology's conditions.

## What do the three results mean?

| Result | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pass | The input you gave satisfies the condition as the methodology states it. | Make sure the evidence behind the input is uploaded. The validator will ask for it. |
| Fail | The input you gave does not satisfy the condition. | Check the input. If it is correct, the project does not fit this methodology as described. |
| Needs review | The condition calls for judgment, or its input has not been supplied. | A person on your team has to make the determination and record why. |

## Which conditions are sent to a person?

Some conditions are thresholds: a density, a date, a capacity. Those can be computed. Others ask whether an arrangement meets a description, and turn on facts a form cannot capture. Climat marks those as needs review and does not attempt an answer.

For background on how validators read these conditions, see the guide to [applicability conditions](https://climat.today/guides/applicability-conditions/).

## Which methodologies does it cover?

The check covers the methodologies Climat supports today: [Verra VM0047](https://climat.today/methodologies/vm0047/) version 1.1, census-based approach, and [Verra VMR0017](https://climat.today/methodologies/vmr0017/) version 1.0. Conditions are set up from the published methodology text.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the applicability check done by a language model?

No. The check is rule-based. Each condition is written down from the published methodology with the input it depends on and the test it applies, and the result is computed from your intake. The same inputs always give the same result.

### What happens if an input has not been provided yet?

The condition is reported as needs review. A condition is never reported as passed because its input is missing.

### What should I do if a condition fails?

A failed condition means the project, as described, does not fit the methodology. Check the input first. If it is right, the options are a different methodology, a change to the project, or a deviation under the registry's own rules, which a validator has to accept.

# Document drafting

> Climat drafts each section of the registry's project document from the project's own intake and uploaded evidence. Every statement cites its origin: the intake, an excerpt of the evidence, or the methodology. Citations to uploads are checked against the text supplied, conflicts are raised as warnings, and a person finalizes every section.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/product/document-drafting/

## What does Climat draft?

It drafts the project document the registry requires: the project description under the Verra Verified Carbon Standard, or the project design document under the Gold Standard for the Global Goals. Sections are written in the registry's own order, and the two registries do not ask for the same sections. See [the VCS project description](https://climat.today/registries/verra-vcs/) and [the Gold Standard PDD](https://climat.today/registries/gold-standard/).

DraftSection 4 of 10

Demonstration of Additionality

Regulatory surplus: no statute requires planting on the project parcels `SRC-4`.

Investment analysis: **evidence needed.** No financial model was supplied, so no return figure is stated.

Illustrative example. Where evidence is missing, the draft says so.

## Where does each statement come from?

Every statement in a draft points to one of three places.

| Citation points to | Example | How it is checked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The intake | Project area, planting density, installed capacity | The value is the one you entered |
| An excerpt of your evidence | A page of a land record, a row of a census | The excerpt named must be one that was supplied, or the citation is flagged |
| The methodology | A condition, an equation, a required parameter | Drawn from the methodology as set up from its published text |

## What happens when the intake and the evidence disagree?

The disagreement is raised as a warning on the section it affects. If the intake says two species were planted and the uploaded census shows three, the draft does not pick one. It tells you, with the figures, so that you can correct whichever is wrong.

## What happens when evidence is missing?

The section says so. An additionality test with no supporting document is marked as needing evidence. The draft does not fill the gap with a plausible figure. The same gaps appear earlier, in the evidence gap report, so that most of them can be closed before drafting starts.

## Who has the last word?

You do. Each section is read, edited and finalized by a person. A finalized section is never regenerated. For background on what each section has to establish, see [what a project design document is](https://climat.today/guides/what-is-a-pdd/).

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a citation checked against?

A citation to an uploaded document names an excerpt of that document. Climat checks that the excerpt named is one that was actually supplied to the draft. If it is not, the citation is marked unverified and the section is flagged for review.

### Can I change a section after it is drafted?

Yes. You can edit the text directly or ask for a rewrite with your own instructions. Once you finalize a section, it is left alone: drafting the rest of the document again will not touch it.

### Does Climat write the numbers in the quantification section?

It sets out the structure the methodology requires and the parameters involved, and it uses the values you supplied. It does not invent a value for a parameter that has no source.

# Monitoring periods

> After a project is registered, it has to collect the data its methodology requires and report it for each monitoring period. Climat's monitoring tracking is in development: it is built and tested in the engine, and is not yet available to users.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/product/monitoring/

In development

## What is a monitoring period?

A monitoring period is the span of time covered by one monitoring report. During it, the project collects the data its methodology lists as monitored parameters. At the end, that data is reported and verified before credits are issued for the period.

## What will Climat's monitoring do?

- **Open the periods.** Once a project is registered, the crediting period will be divided into monitoring periods at the cadence the project sets.

- **Carry the parameters in.** Each period will hold its own copy of the methodology's monitoring parameters, with the frequency the methodology states.

- **Record values and evidence.** Your team will record a value and its supporting evidence for each parameter, or a reason why a parameter does not apply.

- **Refuse an incomplete period.** A period with a parameter that has no value will not be submitted, and the report will name what is outstanding.

## What is available today?

Everything up to a finished project document is available now. See [how Climat works](https://climat.today/product/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is monitoring available in Climat today?

Not yet. Monitoring tracking is in development. It is built and tested in the engine, and its screens are being added.

### Will Climat collect monitoring data from sensors or satellites?

No. It will track the values and evidence your team records for each parameter. It is not a measurement system.
