URL: https://climat.today/product/pre-validation/

# Pre-validation review

> Pre-validation is a critical review of a project document carried out before it is submitted to a validation and verification body, so that likely findings are fixed first. Climat's pre-validation review is in development: it is built and tested in the engine, and is not yet available to users.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/product/pre-validation/

In development

## What is pre-validation?

Pre-validation is a review of the project document before it goes to the validator. Its purpose is to find the issues a validation and verification body is likely to raise, while they are still cheap to fix. A finding raised during validation costs a round trip: the validator writes it up, the developer responds, the validator reviews the response. For how that process runs, see [validation and verification](https://climat.today/guides/validation-and-verification/).

## What will Climat's review do?

It will read the finished draft adversarially, one section at a time, with the methodology's own conditions and the other sections in view. Each finding will have four parts.

| Part | What it contains |
| --- | --- |
| Claim | The exact words of the document that are being challenged, quoted word for word |
| Issue | What is wrong or unsupported, and why a validator would raise it |
| Remedy | What would resolve it: a source, a correction, a document |
| Severity | Blocking, material or advisory |

## How will findings be graded?

| Severity | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Blocking | The document would fail validation on this point alone |
| Material | Likely to be raised by a validator, and will cost a round trip |
| Advisory | Would strengthen the case, but is not a likely finding |

## What kinds of problem will it look for?

- **Unsupported claim.** Something asserted with no citation.

- **Evidence gap.** Something cited to evidence that does not exist yet.

- **Methodology deviation.** Something that conflicts with the methodology's own rules.

- **Internal inconsistency.** Something that contradicts another section or the intake.

- **Registry requirement.** Something the registry asks for that the section leaves out.

- **Calculation.** An arithmetic or unit error.

## What is available today instead?

Three checks that catch many of the same problems earlier are available now: the [applicability check](https://climat.today/product/applicability-check/), the evidence gap report, and the citation checks and conflict warnings in [document drafting](https://climat.today/product/document-drafting/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is pre-validation available in Climat today?

Not yet. The review is in development. It is built and tested in the engine, and its screens are being added. We will say so on this page when it can be used.

### Is pre-validation a substitute for validation?

No. Validation is carried out by a validation and verification body approved by the registry, and only that body's opinion counts. Pre-validation is a self-review that aims to reduce the number of findings the validator has to raise.

### Will the review always find something?

No. A section that is sound should produce no findings, and the review is designed to return an empty list when that is the honest answer.

---

URL: https://climat.today/registries/

# Registries

> Each carbon standard requires its own project document, with its own sections in its own order. These pages set out what the Verra Verified Carbon Standard and the Gold Standard for the Global Goals each ask a project developer to write, and the program rules that shape a project's timeline.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/registries/

## Why does the registry matter to the document?

The same project, under the same kind of methodology, produces a different document at each registry. Gold Standard asks for an assessment against its safeguarding principles, a stakeholder consultation report and stated contributions to the Sustainable Development Goals. The Verified Carbon Standard does not ask for those in the same form. A document written for one registry and relabeled for the other will be missing sections.

For a side by side comparison, see [Verra VCS vs Gold Standard](https://climat.today/guides/verra-vs-gold-standard/).

---

URL: https://climat.today/registries/gold-standard/

# The Gold Standard PDD: every section and what it must establish

> A Gold Standard for the Global Goals project is documented in the Project Design Document template v2.0 of 15 May 2026: key project information, a project impact summary, and sections A to I. The PDD must show methodology compliance, a safeguarding assessment, a stakeholder consultation, and monitored contributions to at least three Sustainable Development Goals, including SDG 13.

Updated 2026-09-30. Canonical: https://climat.today/registries/gold-standard/

- **Core standard:** Principles & Requirements v2.1, published 31 January 2025, effective 5 December 2024
- **Current PDD template:** Project Design Document template v2.0, 15 May 2026
- **Template structure:** Key project information, project impact summary, and sections A to I
- **Sustainable Development Goals:** At least three, one of which must be SDG 13
- **Certification cycle:** Five years, renewable; 15 years in total for renewable energy and community services, 30 to 50 years for afforestation and reforestation
- **First submission deadline:** Preliminary review within one year of the project start date
- **Review fees (Fee Schedule v3.1):** USD 1,000 preliminary review, USD 2,500 design review, USD 2,000 performance review

## Which documents govern a Gold Standard for the Global Goals project?

Every project applies the Principles & Requirements and the documents associated with them. It then applies the activity requirements for its project type and, if it seeks credits, the methodology and the product requirements. Section 1.3 of the [Principles & Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/) sets that order.

| Document | Current version | What it governs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Principles & Requirements | v2.1, published 31 January 2025, effective 5 December 2024 | Eligibility, the five principles, the project cycle and the project documentation |
| [Safeguarding Principles & Requirements](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/103-par-safeguarding-principles-requirements/) | v2.1, published 29 June 2023 | The assessment against nine safeguarding principles |
| [Stakeholder Consultation and Engagement Requirements](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/102-par-stakeholder-consultation-requirements/) | v2.1, published 14 June 2022 | The two consultation rounds and the grievance mechanism |
| [GHG Emissions Reduction & Sequestration Product Requirements](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/501-pr-ghg-emissions-reductions-sequestration/) | v3.2, published 12 December 2025 | Issuance of Gold Standard Verified Emission Reductions (GSVERs): eligible gases, project scale, crediting period, double counting |
| Activity requirements for the project type | [Community Services v1.2](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/201-ar-community-services-activity-requirements/) (October 2019), [Renewable Energy v1.4](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/202-ar-renewable-energy-activity-requirements/) (16 August 2021), [Land Use & Forests v1.2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/203-ar-luf-activity-requirements/) (April 2020) | Eligibility, crediting period and additionality rules for the project type |
| [Requirements for Paris Agreement Alignment](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/119_paa_pr_100-01-requirements-paris-agreement-alignment/) | v1.1, published 2 February 2026 | The methodology a project may apply for credits of vintage 2026 onward |

A project submitted for preliminary review after 30 June 2026 must apply a Paris Agreement aligned methodology (Requirements for Paris Agreement Alignment, section 4.1.1). Where no activity requirements exist for a project type, the Principles & Requirements apply on their own (section 1.3.2). The PDD template also lists blue carbon and freshwater wetlands, and engineered removal, as activity requirement categories. Those documents are not summarized here.

## Which PDD template is current?

The current template is the [Project Design Document template v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/t-prereview-design-document/), dated 15 May 2026. The previous version is v1.5 of 29 June 2023. The template is written for a standalone project activity.

The document history of v2.0 records structural changes, reporting space for new requirements such as Paris Agreement alignment, and specific reporting on safeguarding, stakeholder consultation and gender. Gold Standard's template page says developers may use the older templates for vintages that are not Paris Agreement aligned, and may use the new forms voluntarily in any case.

Section 6.1.1 of the Principles & Requirements requires approved Gold Standard templates for everything except supporting evidence. The template asks for the PDD as a non-editable PDF and sets a file name for each stage, for example `GSID_PDD_DDMMYYYY_VER_X` at design review. For what a PDD is and how other standards name it, see [what is a project design document](https://climat.today/guides/what-is-a-pdd/).

## What does each section of the PDD template have to establish?

Template v2.0 has three unnumbered opening blocks, then sections A to I. The table follows the template's order.

| Section | What it has to establish |
| --- | --- |
| Key project information | Host country, developer, scale, regular or retroactive project cycle, reductions or removals, the activity requirement, the methodologies with their versions, and the product requirements applied. |
| Transition details | Only for a project moving from the CDM, the Article 6.4 mechanism or another standard: its status there, and a declaration that each vintage is issued under one standard only. |
| Project impact summary | Annual emission reductions or removals, the SDGs claimed, and checklists for safeguarding, gender equality, stakeholder consultation and benefit sharing. |
| A. Project description | A.1 overview. A.2 location. A.3 technology or measures, and any existing or former project at the same location. A.4 funding, product ownership and benefit sharing. A.5 eligibility and double counting risks. A.6 alignment with national climate and development policies. A.7 start date, operational lifetime and crediting period. |
| B. Application of methodology(ies) | B.1 methodologies applied. B.2 each [applicability condition](https://climat.today/guides/applicability-conditions/), justified per methodology and tool. B.3 project boundary, sources, sinks and gases. B.4 baseline scenario, and business-as-usual scenario or reference benchmark. B.5 [additionality](https://climat.today/guides/additionality/): prior consideration, regulatory surplus, avoidance of lock-in, financial additionality or a performance-based approach, common practice, ongoing financial need. B.6 non-permanence and risk of reversals. B.7 emission reductions or net removals: baseline and its downward adjustment, project emissions, leakage, parameters fixed ex ante, buffer. B.8 monitoring plan, sampling plan, monitoring management system. |
| C. Safeguarding principles and gender sensitivity assessment | C.1 the risks identified under each safeguarding principle, with monitoring indicators. C.2 the mitigation and monitoring plan. |
| D. Gender equality assessment | D.1 how the project meets the gender sensitive requirements, which are mandatory, and the gender responsive ones if sought. D.2 the monitoring plan. |
| E. Sustainable development contribution | E.1 that SDG 13 and two more SDGs are identified. E.2 the contributions and their alignment with host country objectives. E.3 a monitoring parameter for each, with baseline value, project value and net benefit. |
| F. Stakeholder consultation assessment | A summary of the consultation: F.1 scope, F.2 stakeholders invited, F.3 modalities, F.4 comments received, F.5 how they were considered, F.6 the continuous input and grievance mechanism. |
| G. Contact information of project developer | Organization, address and contact person. |
| H. Appendices | H.1 applicability of methodologies. H.2 background to the ex ante calculation. H.3 monitoring plan details. H.4 changes to a design certified project. H.5 voluntary disclosure of intended co-benefits. |
| I. LUF additional information | For land use and forests projects: land-use history, forest management, social and environmental impacts, and the sites and rights of indigenous people and local communities. |

Several tables in sections C and E are filled in only if the developer has not used Gold Standard's Digital SDG Impact Tool. If the tool was used, its assessment file is uploaded to the Gold Standard Assurance Platform.

## What is specific to Gold Standard?

Three things: a safeguarding assessment, a stakeholder consultation, and monitored contributions to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Certified design status means the project has met all three and has a compliant monitoring plan ([Principles & Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/), section 2.1.1).

### The safeguarding assessment

The [Safeguarding Principles & Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/103-par-safeguarding-principles-requirements/) set nine principles, from human rights to environment, ecology and land use. Every assessment question must be answered (section 5.1.1), with yes, potentially, no or not applicable (Annex 1). A *yes* puts the requirement into the monitoring plan. A *potentially* is updated in every monitoring report. Where host country law and the Gold Standard requirement differ, the more stringent applies (section 4.1.2).

### The stakeholder consultation

The [Stakeholder Consultation and Engagement Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/102-par-stakeholder-consultation-requirements/) require at least two rounds: a physical meeting and a feedback round of at least 30 days (section 3.6.1). Invitations go out at least 30 days before the meeting (section 3.4.2). A consultation held before the project start date makes the project regular. One held after makes it retroactive (Principles & Requirements, section 4.1.42). A grievance mechanism runs for the project's lifetime (section 3.8.1). The full report, on its own template, is due within one year of the start date (Principles & Requirements, section 4.1.35).

### The SDG contributions and their monitoring

A project must show positive impacts on at least three SDGs, one of which must be SDG 13 (Principles & Requirements, section 4.1.12). Each impact must be a direct, intentional effect of the project, measured against the baseline scenario (sections 4.1.13 and 4.1.14). The Monitoring & Reporting Plan in the PDD states the metric, frequency, collection method and quality control for every parameter (section 4.1.44).

## Which program rules does a developer have to plan around?

Four sets of rules shape the timeline: the crediting period, the deadline for first submission, the certification steps, and the routes for changing a certified design.

### Crediting period and renewal

Certification runs in five-year cycles. Renewal updates the project information and the baseline, unless the activity requirements say otherwise ([Principles & Requirements v2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/101-par-principles-requirements/), section 5.1.1). The activity requirements set the total.

| Project type | Total crediting period | Clause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Renewable energy | 15 years | [Renewable Energy Activity Requirements v1.4](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/202-ar-renewable-energy-activity-requirements/), section 4.4.2 |
| Community services | 15 years | [Community Services Activity Requirements v1.2](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/201-ar-community-services-activity-requirements/), section 4.1.5 |
| Afforestation and reforestation | 30 to 50 years, chosen by the developer | [Land Use & Forests Activity Requirements v1.2.1](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/203-ar-luf-activity-requirements/), section 3.1.9 |
| Agriculture | Fixed 10 years, unless the methodology states otherwise | Land Use & Forests Activity Requirements v1.2.1, section 3.1.10 |
| No limit in the activity requirements | 10 years, with one renewal | Principles & Requirements v2.1, section 5.1.1(f); [GHG Product Requirements v3.2](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/501-pr-ghg-emissions-reductions-sequestration/), section 10.1.1 |

The VVB's renewal opinion must reach Gold Standard by the last day of the current cycle, and a delay reduces issuance in the next cycle (sections 5.1.45 and 5.1.46). A certified forestry or mangrove project managed as conservation forest can extend its period to a maximum of 50 years through a design change ([Extension of Crediting Period requirements v1.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/117_par_extension-of-crediting-period-luf/), sections 4.1.1 and 4.1.6).

### Deadline for first submission

A project must be submitted for preliminary review within one year of its start date, the earliest date on which the developer committed to expenditure on implementation (Principles & Requirements, sections 4.1.39 and 4.1.49). A retroactive project submitted later is not eligible. Section 4.1.49 does not state the consequence for a regular project. Retroactive land use and forests projects have five years (Land Use & Forests Activity Requirements, section 3.1.14).

### Certification steps

Section numbers refer to the Principles & Requirements v2.1.

1. **Preliminary review.** Gold Standard reviews the key project information and the draft stakeholder consultation report, with a completeness check within 14 days. A draft PDD is required only for a new project type, methodology or product (sections 5.1.4 and 5.1.8). The result is Listed status, which is not certification (section 5.1.12).

2. **Validation and design review.** An approved VVB validates the complete PDD within two years of listing (section 5.1.16). Gold Standard's design review lasts at least four weeks and includes a two-week public consultation (sections 5.1.19 and 5.1.21).

3. **Verification and performance review.** The first verification is due within two years of implementation or design certification, whichever is later (section 5.1.29). The performance review lasts at least three weeks (section 5.1.34).

For the full sequence, see [how to register a carbon project](https://climat.today/guides/how-to-register-a-carbon-project/) and [validation and verification](https://climat.today/guides/validation-and-verification/).

### Design changes and deviations

A permanent change to a certified design needs a design change request: a revised PDD in track-change and clean versions and, unless stated otherwise, a positive VVB opinion ([Design Change Request Requirements and Procedures v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/111-par-design-change-requirements/), sections 2.1.4 and 2.1.6). A rejected request blocks issuance until the earlier design is restored or another change is accepted (section 6.1.9). A temporary change, or a deviation sought before submission for certification, follows the [Deviation Request Requirements and Procedures v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/110-par-deviation-approval-procedure/) (section 1.1.1). Where no precedent exists, Gold Standard's Technical Advisory Committee decides, in four to eight weeks (section 5.2).

## How Climat handles this

Climat seeds Gold Standard as its own document, with its own section list and its own order, because the drafting order belongs to the registry. For Gold Standard that seed is nine sections: project description, safeguarding principles and requirements assessment, stakeholder consultation report, sustainable development goal contributions, application of methodology, additionality, baseline scenario and emission reductions, monitoring plan, and crediting period. Safeguards, consultation and SDG contributions sit near the front, where Gold Standard puts them, rather than near the back as they do under VCS.

That list is a working decomposition, not the template. The [Project Design Document template v2.0](https://globalgoals.goldstandard.org/t-prereview-design-document/) is the authority, and a person maps Climat's sections onto its key project information block, its project impact summary and its sections A to I before anything is submitted. Two things Climat cannot do for a developer are worth naming: the safeguarding assessment and the stakeholder consultation both rest on evidence gathered outside the document — a physical meeting, a feedback round, a grievance mechanism — and Climat can only draft the record of what was done and flag what is missing. It does not run the consultation, and it is neither a registry nor a validation and verification body.

Our [comparison of the two registries](https://climat.today/guides/verra-vs-gold-standard/) sets out where the choice actually bites, and [what a project design document is](https://climat.today/guides/what-is-a-pdd/) covers the material both registries want.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long is the crediting period for a Gold Standard project?

It depends on the project type. Gold Standard certifies in five-year cycles that must be renewed, and the activity requirements cap the total: 15 years for renewable energy and community services projects, a fixed 10 years for agriculture, and 30 to 50 years for afforestation and reforestation. Where no activity requirement sets a limit, the Principles & Requirements v2.1 allow one renewal, which gives 10 years.

### How soon after the project start date must a project be submitted to Gold Standard?

Within one year. Section 4.1.49 of the Principles & Requirements v2.1 requires regular and retroactive projects to submit for preliminary review within one year of the project start date, and a retroactive project submitted later is not eligible. Retroactive land use and forests projects have five years under the Land Use & Forests Activity Requirements v1.2.1. The deadline applies to the first submission, not to design certification.

### Is the stakeholder consultation report part of the Gold Standard PDD?

No. It is a separate document, written on Gold Standard's Stakeholder Consultation Report template. Section F of the PDD template v2.0 holds a summary of the consultation and the final grievance mechanism, and refers to the separate report for the full record. The complete report, covering both consultation rounds, is due within one year of the project start date.

### How many Sustainable Development Goals must a Gold Standard project contribute to?

At least three, and one of them must be SDG 13, climate action. Section 4.1.12 of the Principles & Requirements v2.1 sets the minimum, and section 4.1.13 requires each impact to be an intentional, direct effect of the project. The PDD must identify the monitoring indicators for each impact and define how they are monitored.

### What is the difference between a design change and a deviation under Gold Standard?

A design change is permanent and a deviation is temporary. Permanent changes to the implementation, operation or monitoring of a certified project follow the Design Change Request Requirements and Procedures v2.0 and need a revised PDD. Deviations from requirements or methodologies before submission for certification, and temporary changes that will not last beyond a monitoring period, follow the Deviation Request Requirements and Procedures v2.0.

### What does Gold Standard charge to certify a project?

Under the Fee Schedule v3.1 of 28 July 2025, the preliminary review costs USD 1,000, the design review USD 2,500 and each performance review USD 2,000. Issuance costs USD 0.25 per credit in cash, or USD 0.15 per credit plus 2 percent of the issuance. A registry account costs USD 1,000 a year per organization.

# The Verra VCS project description: every section and what it must establish

> The Verra VCS project description is written on VCS Project Description Template v5.0A or v5.0B, both issued 9 June 2026. Each has five numbered sections (project details, safeguards and stakeholder engagement, application of methodology, quantification, monitoring) and two standing appendices. A project start date before 1 January 2027 means v5.0A; on or after that date, v5.0B.

Updated 2026-09-30. Canonical: https://climat.today/registries/verra-vcs/

- **Current edition:** VCS Version 5, released 16 December 2025
- **Templates:** VCS Project Description Template v5.0A and v5.0B, issued 9 June 2026, effective 1 January 2027
- **Which template:** v5.0A for a project start date before 1 January 2027; v5.0B on or after that date
- **Structure:** 5 numbered sections and 2 standing appendices; 36 numbered subsections in v5.0A, 37 in v5.0B
- **Crediting period (VCS Standard v5.0, section 3.8.4):** 5 years for energy and industry, geological carbon storage, livestock systems, and agricultural land management without soil organic carbon stock change; 20 to 100 years for the other AFOLU categories
- **Public comment period:** 30 days, starting when the project is listed as under validation
- **Fees (Verra Program Fee Schedule v1.2):** USD 1,500 pipeline listing, USD 3,750 registration review, USD 0.23 per tCO2e issuance levy

## Which version of the VCS Program is current, and which documents govern a project?

VCS Version 5 is the current edition. Verra released it on 16 December 2025, and section 1.1 of the [VCS Program Guide v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-program-guide-v5-0/) states that it replaces Version 4 as the applicable version. Each update has its own effective date, listed in the [overview of updates and effective dates](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-version-5-overview-of-vcs-program-updates-and-effective-dates/). Verra's [rules page](https://verra.org/programs/verified-carbon-standard/vcs-program-details/) lists the VCS Standard v4.7 as active until 1 January 2027.

| Document | What it governs |
| --- | --- |
| VCS Program Guide v5.0 | The overarching document: program scope, roles, the registry, and how effective dates work |
| [VCS Standard v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v5-0/) | The requirements for developing a project and for validation and verification |
| [Registration and Issuance Process v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/) (RIP) | The procedures for pipeline listing, registration, Verra's review, and issuance of Verified Carbon Units (VCUs) |
| [VCS Methodology Requirements v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-methodology-requirements-v5-0/) | The requirements for methodologies, modules and tools. A project meets them through the methodology it applies |

All four are dated 16 December 2025. The [Corrections and Clarifications of 9 June 2026](https://verra.org/documents/corrections-and-clarifications-cc-to-the-vcs-program-rules-published-9-june-2026/) amend the Standard and the RIP, and the Program Guide requires proponents and validation/verification bodies (VVBs) to apply them.

## Which project description template applies, v5.0A or v5.0B?

The project start date decides. Each template states the rule on its first page. Verra issued both on 9 June 2026, with an effective date of 1 January 2027.

- **[Template v5.0A](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0a/).** A project with a start date before 1 January 2027 that submits a pipeline listing request, a registration request, or, before 1 January 2030, a crediting period renewal request or a verification approval request that includes a baseline reassessment.

- **[Template v5.0B](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-project-description-template-v5-0b/).** A project with a start date on or after 1 January 2027, for any request that requires a project description. Also an earlier project that submits a renewal request, or a verification approval request with a baseline reassessment, on or after 1 January 2030.

The templates differ in the rules they report against. v5.0A applies sections 3.7, 3.18 and 3.19 of the [VCS Standard v4.7](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v4-7/): ownership, stakeholder engagement and safeguards. v5.0B applies sections 3.6, 3.17 and 3.18 of the VCS Standard v5.0. Neither is for a project that must use the digital template in the Verra Project Hub. For what the document is and who reads it, see [what a project design document is](https://climat.today/guides/what-is-a-pdd/).

## What does each section of the project description have to establish?

The table follows Template v5.0A, in the template's own order and with Verra's section names. The template's instructions are mandatory. A section that does not apply is explained and justified, not deleted.

| Section (v5.0A) | What it has to establish |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Project Details | What the project is, who runs it, and that it is eligible |
| 1.1 Summary Description of the Project | In one page: technologies or measures, location, how reductions or removals arise, the prior scenario, estimated annual and total volumes |
| 1.2 Audit History | Every audit to date and the forthcoming one |
| 1.3 Sectoral Scope and Project Classification | Sectoral scope, project category and project activity type |
| 1.4 Project Eligibility | Listing and registration deadlines met; eligibility of agriculture, forestry and other land use (AFOLU) projects; status under any other GHG program; not a fragment of a larger project under a capacity limit |
| 1.5 Project Proponent | Organization and contact for each proponent |
| 1.6 Other Entities Involved in the Project | Every other entity and its part in implementation, management and monitoring |
| 1.7 Ownership | How project ownership is established, with the evidence |
| 1.8 Project Start Date and Initial Crediting Period Start Date | Both dates, and the significant action that fixes the start date |
| 1.9 Project Crediting Period | Length, start and end dates, period number, maximum total duration |
| 1.10 Project Scale | Project or large project (over 300,000 tCO2e a year), with an estimate for each calendar year |
| 1.11 Project Design | Single instance, multiple instances, grouped project or expanding geological carbon storage (GCS) project; for a grouped project, the eligibility areas and criteria for adding instances |
| 1.12 Conditions Prior to Project Initiation | Existing facilities and equipment, or for AFOLU the ecosystem type, land use and environmental conditions |
| 1.13 Description of the Project Activity | Technologies or measures, how they achieve the reductions or removals, and the implementation schedule |
| 1.14 Project Location | Country down to municipality, maps, and a geolocation file attached separately |
| 1.15 Compliance with Laws and Other Regulatory Frameworks | Each relevant law and how the project complies; screening for politically exposed and sanctioned persons |
| 1.16 Double Counting and Participation with Other GHG Programs | No double issuance; any registration with, or rejection by, another GHG program |
| 1.17 Double Claiming, Other Forms of Credit, and Scope 3 Emissions | No double claiming under an emissions trading program, a binding limit or another environmental credit; supply chain emissions |
| 1.18 Sustainable Development Contributions | Each contribution, with its Sustainable Development Goal target, indicator, baseline and expected result |
| 1.19 Additional Information | Leakage management, whether information is withheld as sensitive, and anything else bearing on eligibility or quantification |
| 2 Safeguards and Stakeholder Engagement | That people and ecosystems were consulted and protected, under the VCS Standard v4.7 |
| 2.1 Stakeholder Engagement and Consultation | Stakeholder identification, consultation and ongoing communication, free, prior and informed consent (FPIC), the grievance redress procedure, and public comments with the action taken |
| 2.2 Risks to Stakeholders and the Environment | Management experience, the risks identified, and mitigation measures |
| 2.3 Respect for Human Rights and Equity | Risks and mitigation for labor, human rights, Indigenous Peoples and cultural heritage, and property rights; benefit sharing |
| 2.4 Ecosystem Health | Risks to biodiversity, soil and water; rare, threatened and endangered species; species introduced; ecosystem conversion |
| 3 Application of Methodology | That the methodology fits, and what follows from it |
| 3.1 Methodology Details | Each methodology, module and tool applied, with ID and version |
| 3.2 Applicability and Eligibility of Methodology | That each is listed by Verra and active when the request is submitted; every [applicability condition](https://climat.today/guides/applicability-conditions/) justified separately |
| 3.3 Project Boundary | Carbon pools, and GHG sources and sinks for baseline, project and leakage; anything deemed de minimis |
| 3.4 Baseline Scenario | The method used, applied step by step, with the outcome of each step; baseline reassessment when due |
| 3.5 Additionality | Regulatory surplus, then the [additionality](https://climat.today/guides/additionality/) method, with enough data to reproduce the analysis |
| 3.6 Methodology Deviations | Each deviation, its justification, and that it concerns only monitoring or measurement |
| 4 Quantification of Estimated Reductions and Removals | The ex-ante numbers, reproducible by a reader |
| 4.1 Baseline Emissions, 4.2 Project Emissions, 4.3 Leakage Emissions | For each: procedures, numbered equations, justified choices, and enough information to reproduce the calculation |
| 4.4 Other Relevant Quantification | Non-permanence risk rating, buffer pool allocation, and the long-term average for afforestation, reforestation and revegetation (ARR) and improved forest management (IFM) projects with harvesting |
| 4.5 Estimated GHG Emission Reductions and Carbon Dioxide Removals | Net estimates for each vintage period, with reductions and removals separated where the methodology allows |
| 5 Monitoring | How the data will be collected and controlled |
| 5.1 Data and Parameters | A cross-reference to Appendix 2 |
| 5.2 Monitoring Plan | Data collection and management, calibration, personnel, internal auditing and QA/QC, non-conformances, sampling |
| Appendix 1: Sensitive Information | What is withheld from the public version, and why it qualifies |
| Appendix 2: Data and Parameters | Each parameter fixed at validation (A2.1) and each parameter monitored (A2.2) |

## How does a project get from listing to registration?

The [Registration and Issuance Process, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/registration-and-issuance-process-v5-0/), splits the path into a pipeline listing stage and a registration stage, and the project description is written twice over.

1. **Listing as under development.** A partial project description is enough, and indicative figures are acceptable. The file is submitted as `VCS_PD_DRAFT`. Verra charges USD 1,500 for each pipeline listing request.

2. **Listing as under validation.** The proponent submits the full documentation set, including a completed project description, to move the status on (Section 3.1.16). A second listing representation is not required.

3. **The 30-day public comment period.** It starts on the date the status becomes *under validation*, and the project stays on the pipeline as under validation for the whole 30 days (Section 3.1.17). Comments go through the Verra Project Hub; respondents give a name, organization, country and email address. Verra shares every comment with the proponent at the end, posts a public summary, and the proponent addresses them as the VCS Standard requires.

4. **Validation.** Once the comment period completes, the validation and verification body may conclude validation (Section 3.1.20). Validation has to be complete before registration is requested (Section 4.1.1).

5. **Registration review.** The registration request costs USD 3,750. Verification approval follows on its own track, and a proponent must submit a verification approval request within five years of the approval date of the registration request or of the most recent verification approval request (Section 4.1.2).

A project that stops responding loses its place: Verra may reject a project where it receives no reactivation request within 12 months of the status changing to inactive, and from 15 April 2026 it began inactivating pipeline projects that do not respond to findings within 90 days at the listing stage.

## Which crediting period applies?

Table 8 in section 3.8.4 of the [VCS Standard, v5.0](https://verra.org/documents/vcs-standard-v5-0/), sets the length by project type, and the change lands with registration requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027.

| Project type | Crediting period | Times renewable | Maximum total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ALM with SOC stock change, ARR, IFM, REDD, WRC, ACoGS | 20–100 years | 4 | 100 years |
| Geological carbon storage (GCS) | 5 years | 8 | 45 years |
| Energy and industry (E&I), ALM without SOC stock change, livestock systems | 5 years | 2 | 15 years |

Verra's stated reason for the five-year periods is to make projects update to an active methodology and reassess their baselines more often. For the long AFOLU periods, baseline reassessment intervals were shortened to five years, or to whatever the applied methodology sets. For geological carbon storage the five-year renewal and the 45-year maximum took effect immediately for projects that initiated listing on or after 16 December 2025, and at the first renewal request for those listed before it. A renewal request has to reach Verra within two years of the end of the previous crediting period, or within two years of Verra approving a new methodology where the project is switching to one (Section 3.8.9).

## What does it cost?

From the [Verra Program Fee Schedule, v1.2](https://verra.org/documents/verra-program-fee-schedule-v1-2/). These are registry fees only: they exclude the validation and verification body's own fees, which are negotiated with the VVB and are usually the larger number.

| Fee | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| Registry account opening | USD 750 per account |
| Annual account maintenance | USD 750 per account |
| Pipeline listing | USD 1,500 per request |
| Registration review | USD 3,750 per request |
| Verification review | USD 5,000 per request — USD 2,500 review fee plus a USD 2,500 prepayment credited against future issuances |
| VCU issuance levy | USD 0.23 per claimed tCO 2 e of reductions or removals |

Two fees are worth planning for separately. The prepayment means a project pays no issuance fee on its first USD 2,500-worth of VCUs, and it is not charged again if a returned verification request is resubmitted. And projects using module VMD0055 for avoided unplanned deforestation pay a project activity data allocation fee of USD 10,000 per request plus USD 0.25 per hectare in the submitted KML, capped at USD 150,000 per project.

## How Climat handles this

Climat drafts against a seeded description of the registry's document rather than against the PDF template. For VCS that seed is a ten-section list — project description, project boundary, application of the methodology, demonstration of additionality, baseline scenario, quantification, monitoring, data and quality management, environmental and social safeguards, and crediting period — in that order, because the drafting order is the registry's, not ours.

That list is a working decomposition, not the template. Template v5.0A and v5.0B put the same material under five numbered sections and two appendices, and they are the authority: a person maps Climat's sections onto the template's numbered subsections, and fills the title page, the sensitive-information appendix and the data-and-parameters appendix, before anything is submitted. Climat drafts, cites and flags; it does not produce a file for upload to the Verra Project Hub, and it is neither a registry nor a validation and verification body. Our [guide to project design documents](https://climat.today/guides/what-is-a-pdd/) covers what each section has to establish, and [validation and verification](https://climat.today/guides/validation-and-verification/) covers what the VVB does with it.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many sections does the VCS project description template have?

Five numbered sections: Project Details, Safeguards and Stakeholder Engagement, Application of Methodology, Quantification of Estimated Reductions and Removals, and Monitoring. Two standing appendices follow, for sensitive information and for data and parameters. Template v5.0A has 36 numbered subsections and v5.0B has 37, because v5.0B renames the second section Stakeholder Engagement and Safeguards and gives it five subsections instead of four.

### Does a project that started before 2027 ever move to template v5.0B?

Yes. Template v5.0B applies to a project with a start date before 1 January 2027 when it submits a crediting period renewal request, or a verification approval request that includes a baseline reassessment, on or after 1 January 2030. Until then the project reports on v5.0A.

### Which sections must be drafted to list a project as under development?

The Corrections and Clarifications of 9 June 2026 list them for requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027: the title page, sections 1.1 to 1.5, 1.8 to 1.13 and 1.15 to 1.17, the grievance redress section (2.1.4 in v5.0A, 2.4 in v5.0B), and sections 3.1 and 3.2. Indicative information is sufficient at that stage. Listing as under validation requires a project description with all sections completed.

### Does a renewable energy project need a non-permanence risk report?

No. Under section 3.2.8 of the VCS Standard v5.0, non-permanence risk analysis applies only to reductions and removals generated through carbon sinks, and activities that reduce N2O, CH4 or fossil fuel-derived CO2 are not subject to it. The template still keeps the heading: the proponent explains that the section is not applicable.

### How long is the crediting period of a renewable energy project under VCS Version 5?

Five years, renewable twice, for a maximum of 15 years, under Table 8 in section 3.8.4 of the VCS Standard v5.0. Verra's overview of effective dates applies the change to registration requests submitted on or after 1 January 2027. The VCS Standard v4.7 allowed seven years, twice renewable, or ten years fixed.

### In what format is the project description submitted?

As a non-editable PDF, in English. The template sets the file name from the document type, the project ID, the completion date and the version, for example VCS_PD_DRAFT for a listing request as under development and VCS_PD for a registration request. Where the applied methodology has been digitalized, the VCS Standard v5.0 requires the digital template in the Verra Project Hub instead.

# How we use AI

> Climat uses a language model to draft sections of the project document and to compare the intake with the uploaded evidence. The applicability check and the evidence gap report are rule-based and are not generated. Citations are checked, a person finalizes every section, and the use of AI is disclosed to the validation body.

Updated 2026-09-29. Canonical: https://climat.today/trust/

## Where is a language model used?

| Part of the product | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Intake form | Built from the methodology's required inputs. Not generated. |
| Applicability check | Rule-based. Computed from the methodology's conditions and your inputs. |
| Evidence gap report | Rule-based. Computed from what the case needs and what was supplied. |
| Section drafting | Language model, working only from your intake, excerpts of your evidence, and the methodology. |
| Conflict warnings | Language model, comparing the intake with the uploaded evidence. |
| Citation check | Rule-based. A cited excerpt must be one that was supplied. |
| Cover note | Language model, with the disclosure of AI assistance required. |

## How are citations checked?

When a draft cites an uploaded document, it names an excerpt. Climat checks that the excerpt named is one that was actually given to the draft. If it is not, the citation is marked unverified and the section is flagged for review. This catches the most damaging failure of generated text: a reference to a source that was never there.

It does not prove that the source supports the statement. That is what the human review is for.

## What does a person have to do?

Read every section, correct it, and finalize it. Decide every applicability condition that is marked as needing review. Resolve every conflict warning. The document is the project proponent's, and so is the responsibility for what it says.

## Whose model is it, and where is my data processed?

Drafting uses a large language model run by a third-party inference provider. Ask us which provider and model are in use and where they are hosted. We will tell you before you upload anything.

## Is my organization's data kept separate?

Yes. Projects, documents and evidence are scoped to the organization that owns them in the data layer, so that one organization's requests cannot read another's records.

## What can go wrong?

A language model can misread a document, draw a wrong conclusion from a correct source, or state something with more confidence than the evidence allows. The checks above reduce that risk and do not remove it. Treat a draft as a draft.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the applicability check generated by AI?

No. It is computed from the methodology's conditions and your inputs using fixed rules. The same inputs always produce the same result.

### Can a draft contain a claim with no source?

Drafted statements carry citations, and a citation to an uploaded document that cannot be matched to the text supplied is flagged. The review step exists so that a person reads every section before it is finalized. No automated check makes a document correct on its own.

### Does the validator know that AI was used?

Yes. The finished case includes a cover note for the validation and verification body that states that AI assistance was used in preparing the document.
